verses.text: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
The same was in the beginning with God.
All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.
In him was life; and the life was the light of men.
And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.
There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.
The same came for a witness, to bear witness of the Light, that all men through him might believe.
He was not that Light, but was sent to bear witness of that Light.
That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world.
He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world knew him not.
He came unto his own, and his own received him not.
But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:
Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, ( and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
John bare witness of him, and cried, saying, This was he of whom I spake, He that cometh after me is preferred before me: for he was before me.
And of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace.
For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ.
No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him.
And this is the record of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, Who art thou?
And he confessed, and denied not; but confessed, I am not the Christ.
And they asked him, What then? Art thou Elias? And he saith, I am not. Art thou that prophet? And he answered, No.
Then said they unto him, Who art thou? that we may give an answer to them that sent us. What sayest thou of thyself?
He said, I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, Make straight the way of the Lord, as said the prophet Esaias.
And they which were sent were of the Pharisees.
And they asked him, and said unto him, Why baptizest thou then, if thou be not that Christ, nor Elias, neither that prophet?
John answered them, saying, I baptize with water: but there standeth one among you, whom ye know not;
He it is, who coming after me is preferred before me, whose shoe’s latchet I am not worthy to unloose.
These things were done in Bethabara beyond Jordan, where John was baptizing.
The next day John seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.
This is he of whom I said, After me cometh a man which is preferred before me: for he was before me.
And I knew him not: but that he should be made manifest to Israel, therefore am I come baptizing with water.
And John bare record, saying, I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it abode upon him.

And I knew him not: but he that sent me to baptize with water, the same said unto me, Upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending, and remaining on him, the same is he which baptizeth with the Holy Ghost.
And I saw, and bare record that this is the Son of God.
Again the next day after John stood, and two of his disciples;
And looking upon Jesus as he walked, he saith, Behold the Lamb of God!
And the two disciples heard him speak, and they followed Jesus.
Then Jesus turned, and saw them following, and saith unto them, What seek ye? They said unto him, Rabbi, ( which is to say, being interpreted, Master,) where dwellest thou?
He saith unto them, Come and see. They came and saw where he dwelt, and abode with him that day: for it was about the tenth hour.
One of the two which heard John speak, and followed him, was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother.
He first findeth his own brother Simon, and saith unto him, We have found the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ.
And he brought him to Jesus. And when Jesus beheld him, he said, Thou art Simon the son of Jona: thou shalt be called Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone.
The day following Jesus would go forth into Galilee, and findeth Philip, and saith unto him, Follow me.
Now Philip was of Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.
Philip findeth Nathanael, and saith unto him, We have found him, of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, did write, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.
And Nathanael said unto him, Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth? Philip saith unto him, Come and see.
Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and saith of him, Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!
Nathanael saith unto him, Whence knowest thou me? Jesus answered and said unto him, Before that Philip called thee, when thou wast under the fig tree, I saw thee.
Nathanael answered and saith unto him, Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel.
Jesus answered and said unto him, Because I said unto thee, I saw thee under the fig tree, believest thou? thou shalt see greater things than these.
And he saith unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man.

chapters.summary: John begins before creation: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." All things were made by him; "In him was life; and the life was the light of men," a light shining in a darkness that "comprehended it not." John the Baptist is "sent from God" to bear witness to that Light. The Word comes "unto his own, and his own received him not," yet to those who receive him he gives "power to become the sons of God," born not of human will "but of God." Then the hinge: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us," "full of grace and truth," his glory "the glory as of the only begotten of the Father"; where "the law was given by Moses," now "grace and truth came by Jesus Christ," and the unseen God is declared by the Son "which is in the bosom of the Father." Pressed by priests and Levites, John denies being the Christ, Elias, or "that prophet," claiming only to be "the voice of one crying in the wilderness." Seeing Jesus he cries, "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world." Two disciples follow; Jesus asks, "What seek ye?" and answers, "Come and see." Andrew brings Simon, renamed "Cephas"; Philip brings Nathanael, who confesses him "the King of Israel" and is promised sight of "heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man."
takeaways: The prologue identifies Jesus as the eternal Word who both "was with God" and "was God," so the Incarnation is God entering his own creation rather than a creature being promoted into divinity.
"The Word was made flesh" anchors faith in a real human life; the flesh is not a disguise laid over God but the very place where his glory is beheld.
Divine sonship is received, not achieved: the world he made "knew him not," while those who receive him are born "of God" and given power to become his sons.
The Gospel names Jesus "the Lamb of God" before he has said a word, aiming the whole narrative from the start at the sacrifice by which sin is taken away.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 1:1-3 — in the beginning God created, and God said, Let there be light
crossRefs.why: Genesis opens creation with God speaking, with the Spirit over the waters, and with light called out of darkness. John borrows its first three words deliberately, so that the Word through whom "all things were made" is presented as a new beginning inside the old one.

crossRefs.label: Sirach 24:1-12 — Wisdom, created before the world, given a dwelling in Israel
crossRefs.why: Here Wisdom praises herself as created "from the beginning before the world" and is told to make her dwelling in Jacob. Read alongside the prologue it shows the older Jewish language of a pre-existent Wisdom pitching her tent among God's people, which John takes up and personalizes when the Word "dwelt among us."

crossRefs.label: Exodus 33:18-23 — Moses may not see God's face and live
crossRefs.why: Moses asks to see God's glory and is told, "Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live," receiving instead a passing glimpse of goodness. John answers that "No man hath seen God at any time," and that what Moses could not be given the only begotten Son has now made known.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 40:3 — a voice crying in the wilderness, prepare the way of the Lord
crossRefs.why: Isaiah's herald calls for a road to be made straight through the desert for God's own coming. John the Baptist claims this verse as his entire identity, refusing every other title so that nothing about him competes with the one standing unrecognized among them.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 28:10-17 — Jacob's ladder, with the angels of God ascending and descending
crossRefs.why: Jacob dreams of a ladder joining earth to heaven with the angels of God going up and down on it, and wakes to call the place the house of God and the gate of heaven. Jesus promises Nathanael that same vision with himself at the center, presenting the Son of man as the place where heaven and earth now meet.

interpretationNotes.claim: The Catholic tradition reads "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us" as the decisive statement of the Incarnation: one divine person truly taking a complete human nature, so that matter and body become permanent instruments of salvation rather than obstacles to it, a conviction that underwrites the whole sacramental life of the Church.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readers confess the Incarnation with equal force and often press its implications most strongly toward the preached word and personal faith rather than toward sacramental mediation. The difference lies in what follows from the doctrine, not in the doctrine itself. Both traditions hold without reservation that the eternal Word truly became man and that in him alone the unseen God is made known.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition John's cry, "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world," is heard as identifying Jesus with the Passover lamb and the temple offerings, and it is taken up in the liturgy so that the same Lamb once slain is what the worshipper is shown at the altar.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the title as pointing to a single, finished, unrepeatable sacrifice, and are cautious about any liturgical language that could suggest that sacrifice is renewed. Both traditions agree that Jesus is the true and final Lamb, that his death alone takes away sin, and that the phrase is a claim about atonement rather than about mere moral example.

verses.text: And the third day there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee; and the mother of Jesus was there:
And both Jesus was called, and his disciples, to the marriage.
And when they wanted wine, the mother of Jesus saith unto him, They have no wine.
Jesus saith unto her, Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come.
His mother saith unto the servants, Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.
And there were set there six waterpots of stone, after the manner of the purifying of the Jews, containing two or three firkins apiece.
Jesus saith unto them, Fill the waterpots with water. And they filled them up to the brim.
And he saith unto them, Draw out now, and bear unto the governor of the feast. And they bare it.
When the ruler of the feast had tasted the water that was made wine, and knew not whence it was: ( but the servants which drew the water knew;) the governor of the feast called the bridegroom,
And saith unto him, Every man at the beginning doth set forth good wine; and when men have well drunk, then that which is worse: but thou hast kept the good wine until now.
This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him.
After this he went down to Capernaum, he, and his mother, and his brethren, and his disciples: and they continued there not many days.
And the Jews’ passover was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem,
And found in the temple those that sold oxen and sheep and doves, and the changers of money sitting:
And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers’ money, and overthrew the tables;
And said unto them that sold doves, Take these things hence; make not my Father’s house an house of merchandise.
And his disciples remembered that it was written, The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up.
Then answered the Jews and said unto him, What sign shewest thou unto us, seeing that thou doest these things?
Jesus answered and said unto them, Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.
Then said the Jews, Forty and six years was this temple in building, and wilt thou rear it up in three days?
But he spake of the temple of his body.
When therefore he was risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this unto them; and they believed the scripture, and the word which Jesus had said.
Now when he was in Jerusalem at the passover, in the feast day, many believed in his name, when they saw the miracles which he did.
But Jesus did not commit himself unto them, because he knew all men,
And needed not that any should testify of man: for he knew what was in man.

chapters.summary: On "the third day" a wedding at Cana runs out of wine, and the mother of Jesus reports the need: "They have no wine." He answers, "Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come," yet she turns to the servants: "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it." Six stone waterpots "after the manner of the purifying of the Jews" are filled "up to the brim," and what is drawn off is wine so good the steward tells the bridegroom, "thou hast kept the good wine until now." John calls it "This beginning of miracles," by which Jesus "manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him." He then goes up to Jerusalem for the passover and finds the temple courts full of livestock, doves, and "the changers of money sitting." Making "a scourge of small cords," he drives them out and overturns the tables, charging them, "make not my Father's house an house of merchandise," while his disciples recall the words "The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up." Challenged for a sign, he answers, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" — heard as a boast about the building, though "he spake of the temple of his body," a saying believed only after he "was risen from the dead." Many believe at the miracles, but Jesus "did not commit himself unto them," for "he knew what was in man."
takeaways: The first sign is worked at a wedding and in extravagant excess, presenting the arrival of God's reign as a feast and Christ's glory as generous rather than severe.
Mary's role here is intercessory and self-effacing: she names the need without demanding a remedy, and then directs everyone's attention away from herself and toward obedience to her Son.
The temple cleansing shows that worship can be hollowed out from the inside, and that Christ's zeal for his Father's house arrives as judgment before it arrives as comfort.
Jesus relocates the temple into his own body, so that the resurrection rather than any building becomes the sign that vindicates his authority.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 69:9 — the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up
crossRefs.why: The psalm describes a righteous sufferer consumed by zeal for God's house and absorbing the insults aimed at God himself. The disciples remember this verse at the temple cleansing, reading Jesus's action not as a loss of temper but as the opening move of a passion the psalm had already sketched.

crossRefs.label: Malachi 3:1-3 — the Lord suddenly comes to his temple as a refiner
crossRefs.why: Malachi promises that the Lord will come suddenly to his temple like a refiner's fire, purifying the sons of Levi so their offerings can be made in righteousness. Jesus's action in the courts enacts precisely that visitation, which explains both the demand for a sign and the offense the act caused.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 25:6-9 — a feast of wines on the lees, and death swallowed up
crossRefs.why: Isaiah pictures God's final salvation as a mountain banquet of rich food and well refined wine, where the covering over the nations is torn away and death itself is swallowed up. Cana's abundance of good wine reads as a quiet first installment of that promised feast rather than a merely domestic kindness.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 21:12-13 — my house shall be called the house of prayer
crossRefs.why: Matthew places a temple cleansing in the final week and records Jesus quoting the prophets against turning God's house into "a den of thieves." Set beside John's placement of the act at the very start, the two show the whole ministry framed as a conflict over what true worship is.

crossRefs.label: Revelation 19:6-9 — blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb
crossRefs.why: The vision ends the biblical story with a wedding banquet at which the guests are called blessed and the bride is made ready. Cana, where Christ himself supplies the wine at a marriage, anticipates that consummation and gives the first sign its full weight.

interpretationNotes.claim: Cana is read in the Catholic tradition as scriptural ground for Marian intercession: Mary notices the need, presents it to her Son without prescribing a solution, and although told "mine hour is not yet come," her word to the servants immediately precedes the miracle. That Jesus addresses her as "Woman" rather than mother is also read as placing her within the larger story of salvation rather than merely at a village party.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally hear Jesus's reply as a gentle distancing of his mission from family expectation, and read the episode as being about the Son's sovereign timing rather than his mother's influence over it. They note that the text credits the sign entirely to Jesus. Both traditions agree that Mary's last recorded words in Scripture point away from herself: "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it."

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition "the temple of his body" inaugurates a new order of worship centered on the risen body of Christ, which is then extended to the Church as his body and encountered in the Eucharist, so that the temple is not abolished but transposed into a living and still bodily reality.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readers commonly emphasize that the saying announces the end of the temple system altogether, with believers themselves becoming the dwelling place of the Spirit and access to God no longer running through a sanctuary or a priesthood. Both traditions agree that Christ's risen body, not any structure in Jerusalem, is now the place where God is met.

verses.text: There was a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews:
The same came to Jesus by night, and said unto him, Rabbi, we know that thou art a teacher come from God: for no man can do these miracles that thou doest, except God be with him.
Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he can not see the kingdom of God.
Nicodemus saith unto him, How can a man be born when he is old? can he enter the second time into his mother’s womb, and be born?
Jesus answered, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he can not enter into the kingdom of God.
That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.
Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again.
The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit.
Nicodemus answered and said unto him, How can these things be?
Jesus answered and said unto him, Art thou a master of Israel, and knowest not these things?
Verily, verily, I say unto thee, We speak that we do know, and testify that we have seen; and ye receive not our witness.
If I have told you earthly things, and ye believe not, how shall ye believe, if I tell you of heavenly things?
And no man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven, even the Son of man which is in heaven.
And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up:
That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
For God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved.
He that believeth on him is not condemned: but he that believeth not is condemned already, because he hath not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God.
And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil.
For every one that doeth evil hateth the light, neither cometh to the light, lest his deeds should be reproved.
But he that doeth truth cometh to the light, that his deeds may be made manifest, that they are wrought in God.
After these things came Jesus and his disciples into the land of Judæa; and there he tarried with them, and baptized.
And John also was baptizing in Ænon near to Salim, because there was much water there: and they came, and were baptized.
For John was not yet cast into prison.
Then there arose a question between some of John’s disciples and the Jews about purifying.
And they came unto John, and said unto him, Rabbi, he that was with thee beyond Jordan, to whom thou barest witness, behold, the same baptizeth, and all men come to him.
John answered and said, A man can receive nothing, except it be given him from heaven.
Ye yourselves bear me witness, that I said, I am not the Christ, but that I am sent before him.
He that hath the bride is the bridegroom: but the friend of the bridegroom, which standeth and heareth him, rejoiceth greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice: this my joy therefore is fulfilled.
He must increase, but I must decrease.
He that cometh from above is above all: he that is of the earth is earthly, and speaketh of the earth: he that cometh from heaven is above all.
And what he hath seen and heard, that he testifieth; and no man receiveth his testimony.
He that hath received his testimony hath set to his seal that God is true.
For he whom God hath sent speaketh the words of God: for God giveth not the Spirit by measure unto him.
The Father loveth the Son, and hath given all things into his hand.
He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life: and he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him.

chapters.summary: Nicodemus, "a ruler of the Jews," comes to Jesus "by night" and concedes that he is "a teacher come from God." Jesus cuts past the compliment: "Except a man be born again, he can not see the kingdom of God." Nicodemus asks how an old man could re-enter the womb, and Jesus specifies: "Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he can not enter into the kingdom of God," for "That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit," and the Spirit is as untraceable as wind that "bloweth where it listeth." Rebuking "a master of Israel" who knows none of this, Jesus turns to heavenly things: "as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up," leading to "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son." The Son is sent not "to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved," and condemnation proves self-chosen, since "men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil." The scene shifts to the countryside, where both are baptizing. Told that everyone now goes to Jesus, John calls himself only "the friend of the bridegroom," says "He must increase, but I must decrease," and testifies that "he that cometh from heaven is above all," loved by the Father and given "all things into his hand."
takeaways: Entry into the kingdom requires a birth from above rather than an improvement of the birth one already has, and Jesus binds "water" and "the Spirit" together in that single act, tying the Spirit's invisible work to a visible sign.
The cross is the true "lifting up": as with the serpent of brass, the instrument of death becomes the very thing one must look to in order to live.
Judgment in this chapter is exposure rather than sentence — the light arrives, and what a person does with it reveals what he already loved.
John the Baptist models the disciple's proper joy: gladness at being eclipsed, since "A man can receive nothing, except it be given him from heaven."

crossRefs.label: Numbers 21:8-9 — the serpent of brass lifted up on a pole
crossRefs.why: Israel, dying of serpent bites, is healed not by a remedy applied but by looking at a bronze serpent Moses lifts on a pole. Jesus makes this the pattern of his own being "lifted up," so that salvation comes by looking in faith to the very shape of the curse.

crossRefs.label: Ezekiel 36:25-27 — clean water sprinkled, a new heart and a new spirit given
crossRefs.why: God promises to sprinkle clean water for cleansing, to replace the stony heart with a heart of flesh, and to put his own Spirit within his people. This pairing of water and Spirit as God's own act is exactly what "a master of Israel" should have recognized behind Jesus's words about being born again.

crossRefs.label: John 12:32-33 — if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me
crossRefs.why: Later in the Gospel Jesus repeats the phrase and the narrator explains that it signified "what death he should die." The cross-reference settles that "lifted up" in this chapter means crucifixion first, and only through it exaltation.

crossRefs.label: Titus 3:5 — the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost
crossRefs.why: Paul denies that salvation comes by works of righteousness and describes it instead as a washing that regenerates and a renewing worked by the Spirit. Read beside this chapter it shows how early the vocabulary of new birth, water, and Spirit was held together as one gift.

crossRefs.label: 1 John 4:9-10 — not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son
crossRefs.why: The letter restates the sending of the only begotten Son as the definition of love, stressing that the initiative lay entirely with God. It guards this chapter from being read as though belief earned the gift, when belief is the response to a love already given.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition "born of water and of the Spirit" is read as a direct reference to baptism, so that the sacrament is the ordinary means by which the new birth Jesus makes necessary is actually given, and not merely a public illustration of a change already accomplished elsewhere.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters vary: some take "water" as an image of cleansing or of the word, some as John's baptism of repentance being contrasted with the Spirit's work, and most hold that the new birth is worked by the Spirit through faith, with baptism as its sign and seal. Both traditions insist that this birth is God's act from above, impossible for flesh to produce, and both connect it in some way to baptism rather than severing the two.

interpretationNotes.claim: The Catholic tradition reads "For God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved" as expressing a genuinely universal saving will, with the chapter's account of loving darkness explaining condemnation as real human refusal of a grace truly offered.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally affirm the universal offer, though some strands emphasize God's sovereign election and read the chapter's language of "the world" as scope rather than symmetry of intent. Both traditions agree that salvation is entirely God's gift, that no one is condemned for anything but unbelief, and that the light genuinely comes to those who reject it.

verses.text: When therefore the Lord knew how the Pharisees had heard that Jesus made and baptized more disciples than John,
( Though Jesus himself baptized not, but his disciples,)
He left Judæa, and departed again into Galilee.
And he must needs go through Samaria.
Then cometh he to a city of Samaria, which is called Sychar, near to the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph.
Now Jacob’s well was there. Jesus therefore, being wearied with his journey, sat thus on the well: and it was about the sixth hour.
There cometh a woman of Samaria to draw water: Jesus saith unto her, Give me to drink.
( For his disciples were gone away unto the city to buy meat.)
Then saith the woman of Samaria unto him, How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans.
Jesus answered and said unto her, If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water.
The woman saith unto him, Sir, thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep: from whence then hast thou that living water?
Art thou greater than our father Jacob, which gave us the well, and drank thereof himself, and his children, and his cattle?
Jesus answered and said unto her, Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again:
But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.
The woman saith unto him, Sir, give me this water, that I thirst not, neither come hither to draw.
Jesus saith unto her, Go, call thy husband, and come hither.
The woman answered and said, I have no husband. Jesus said unto her, Thou hast well said, I have no husband:
For thou hast had five husbands; and he whom thou now hast is not thy husband: in that saidst thou truly.
The woman saith unto him, Sir, I perceive that thou art a prophet.
Our fathers worshipped in this mountain; and ye say, that in Jerusalem is the place where men ought to worship.
Jesus saith unto her, Woman, believe me, the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father.
Ye worship ye know not what: we know what we worship: for salvation is of the Jews.
But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him.
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
The woman saith unto him, I know that Messias cometh, which is called Christ: when he is come, he will tell us all things.
Jesus saith unto her, I that speak unto thee am he.
And upon this came his disciples, and marvelled that he talked with the woman: yet no man said, What seekest thou? or, Why talkest thou with her?
The woman then left her waterpot, and went her way into the city, and saith to the men,
Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?
Then they went out of the city, and came unto him.
In the mean while his disciples prayed him, saying, Master, eat.
But he said unto them, I have meat to eat that ye know not of.
Therefore said the disciples one to another, Hath any man brought him ought to eat?
Jesus saith unto them, My meat is to do the will of him that sent me, and to finish his work.
Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest? behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest.
And he that reapeth receiveth wages, and gathereth fruit unto life eternal: that both he that soweth and he that reapeth may rejoice together.
And herein is that saying true, One soweth, and another reapeth.
I sent you to reap that whereon ye bestowed no labour: other men laboured, and ye are entered into their labours.
And many of the Samaritans of that city believed on him for the saying of the woman, which testified, He told me all that ever I did.
So when the Samaritans were come unto him, they besought him that he would tarry with them: and he abode there two days.
And many more believed because of his own word;
And said unto the woman, Now we believe, not because of thy saying: for we have heard him ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Christ, the Saviour of the world.
Now after two days he departed thence, and went into Galilee.
For Jesus himself testified, that a prophet hath no honour in his own country.
Then when he was come into Galilee, the Galilæans received him, having seen all the things that he did at Jerusalem at the feast: for they also went unto the feast.
So Jesus came again into Cana of Galilee, where he made the water wine. And there was a certain nobleman, whose son was sick at Capernaum.
When he heard that Jesus was come out of Judæa into Galilee, he went unto him, and besought him that he would come down, and heal his son: for he was at the point of death.
Then said Jesus unto him, Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe.
The nobleman saith unto him, Sir, come down ere my child die.
Jesus saith unto him, Go thy way; thy son liveth. And the man believed the word that Jesus had spoken unto him, and he went his way.
And as he was now going down, his servants met him, and told him, saying, Thy son liveth.
Then enquired he of them the hour when he began to amend. And they said unto him, Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him.
So the father knew that it was at the same hour, in the which Jesus said unto him, Thy son liveth: and himself believed, and his whole house.
This is again the second miracle that Jesus did, when he was come out of Judæa into Galilee.

chapters.summary: Learning that the Pharisees have noticed his growing following, Jesus leaves Judaea and "must needs go through Samaria." At Jacob's well near Sychar, "being wearied with his journey," he sits down about the sixth hour and asks a Samaritan woman, "Give me to drink." She names the barrier at once: "the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans." He offers her instead "living water" that becomes "a well of water springing up into everlasting life"; when she asks for it, he answers by naming her five husbands and her present situation, "in that saidst thou truly." Taking him for a prophet, she raises the old dispute over where God must be worshipped, and Jesus answers that "the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth," since "God is a Spirit." To her hope that "Messias cometh" he replies openly, "I that speak unto thee am he." She leaves her waterpot and tells the city, "Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did." Meanwhile Jesus tells his puzzled disciples, "My meat is to do the will of him that sent me," and points to fields "white already to harvest." Many Samaritans believe first for her word, then "because of his own word," confessing him "the Saviour of the world." Back in Galilee a nobleman begs help for his dying son; Jesus says only, "Thy son liveth," and the fever breaks at that hour.
takeaways: Christ takes the initiative with the outsider and the morally exposed, and the conversation moves from thirst to truth to worship rather than opening with condemnation.
Worship "in spirit and in truth" moves the center of worship from a mountain to a person, without cancelling the claim that "salvation is of the Jews."
The woman's exposure becomes her commission: the first sustained proclamation in Samaria comes from a witness with nothing to boast of, whose testimony is meant to be surpassed by Christ himself.

Faith is drawn from secondhand report toward direct encounter — the Samaritans move from her saying to his own word — and in the nobleman it is stretched to trusting a word before any evidence arrives.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 29:1-12 — Jacob meets Rachel at the well and rolls away the stone
crossRefs.why: Jacob arrives at a well, removes the stone, waters the flock, and the meeting opens a betrothal. John seats Jesus at Jacob's own well asking a woman for water, giving the encounter the shape of a covenant meeting rather than a chance roadside exchange.

crossRefs.label: Jeremiah 2:13 — they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters
crossRefs.why: God charges his people with abandoning him, the fountain of living waters, in order to hew out cracked cisterns that hold nothing. The phrase sharpens Jesus's offer at the well into a claim to be that fountain in person, over against every substitute that cannot satisfy.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 55:1-3 — every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters
crossRefs.why: Isaiah summons the thirsty and the penniless to come and drink without money and without price. Jesus's offer to a woman who has neither standing nor even a vessel he can use enacts that invitation, with the gift depending on nothing she brings.

crossRefs.label: 2 Kings 17:24-34 — the resettling of Samaria and its divided worship
crossRefs.why: This account describes how Samaria was repopulated after the exile and how its inhabitants "feared the LORD, and served their own gods." It supplies the background both to the hostility the woman names and to the force of Jesus's words, "Ye worship ye know not what."

crossRefs.label: Acts 8:5-17 — Christ preached in Samaria, and the Samaritans receive the Spirit
crossRefs.why: After Pentecost the gospel is preached in a city of Samaria, many are baptized, and the Spirit is given. Jesus's two days at Sychar and his talk of fields already white read as the sowing whose reaping the early Church later records.

interpretationNotes.claim: The Catholic tradition reads the "living water" and the promised "well of water springing up into everlasting life" as the indwelling gift of the Spirit and sanctifying grace, ordinarily given through baptism, so that the sign of water at Jacob's well points past physical thirst toward a sacramental life that continues to well up within the believer.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally identify the living water directly with the Spirit received through faith in Christ's word, noting the chapter's own emphasis that the Samaritans came to believe "because of his own word" rather than through any rite. Both traditions agree that the water offered is the Spirit's own life, that Christ alone is its source, and that it is a gift rather than an achievement.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition worship "in spirit and in truth" is read not as a dismissal of external, bodily, and communal worship but as its fulfillment in Christ: the rivalry between two sanctuaries ends because the true sanctuary has arrived in person, and worship in the Spirit is then offered through him in liturgy and sacrament.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readers frequently hear in this verse a decisive turn from place, priesthood, and ceremony toward inward and spiritual worship that may be offered anywhere and by anyone. Both traditions agree that Christ ends the argument about locations by making himself the center of worship, and that the Father is seeking worshippers rather than sites.

verses.text: After this there was a feast of the Jews; and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.
Now there is at Jerusalem by the sheep market a pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, having five porches.
In these lay a great multitude of impotent folk, of blind, halt, withered, waiting for the moving of the water.
For an angel went down at a certain season into the pool, and troubled the water: whosoever then first after the troubling of the water stepped in was made whole of whatsoever disease he had.
And a certain man was there, which had an infirmity thirty and eight years.
When Jesus saw him lie, and knew that he had been now a long time in that case, he saith unto him, Wilt thou be made whole?
The impotent man answered him, Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pool: but while I am coming, another steppeth down before me.
Jesus saith unto him, Rise, take up thy bed, and walk.
And immediately the man was made whole, and took up his bed, and walked: and on the same day was the sabbath.
The Jews therefore said unto him that was cured, It is the sabbath day: it is not lawful for thee to carry thy bed.
He answered them, He that made me whole, the same said unto me, Take up thy bed, and walk.
Then asked they him, What man is that which said unto thee, Take up thy bed, and walk?
And he that was healed wist not who it was: for Jesus had conveyed himself away, a multitude being in that place.
Afterward Jesus findeth him in the temple, and said unto him, Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee.
The man departed, and told the Jews that it was Jesus, which had made him whole.
And therefore did the Jews persecute Jesus, and sought to slay him, because he had done these things on the sabbath day.
But Jesus answered them, My Father worketh hitherto, and I work.
Therefore the Jews sought the more to kill him, because he not only had broken the sabbath, but said also that God was his Father, making himself equal with God.

Then answered Jesus and said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do: for what things soever he doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise.
For the Father loveth the Son, and sheweth him all things that himself doeth: and he will shew him greater works than these, that ye may marvel.
For as the Father raiseth up the dead, and quickeneth them; even so the Son quickeneth whom he will.
For the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment unto the Son:
That all men should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father. He that honoureth not the Son honoureth not the Father which hath sent him.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that heareth my word, and believeth on him that sent me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation; but is passed from death unto life.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God: and they that hear shall live.
For as the Father hath life in himself; so hath he given to the Son to have life in himself;
And hath given him authority to execute judgment also, because he is the Son of man.
Marvel not at this: for the hour is coming, in the which all that are in the graves shall hear his voice,
And shall come forth; they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation.
I can of mine own self do nothing: as I hear, I judge: and my judgment is just; because I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father which hath sent me.
If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true.
There is another that beareth witness of me; and I know that the witness which he witnesseth of me is true.
Ye sent unto John, and he bare witness unto the truth.
But I receive not testimony from man: but these things I say, that ye might be saved.
He was a burning and a shining light: and ye were willing for a season to rejoice in his light.
But I have greater witness than that of John: for the works which the Father hath given me to finish, the same works that I do, bear witness of me, that the Father hath sent me.
And the Father himself, which hath sent me, hath borne witness of me. Ye have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his shape.
And ye have not his word abiding in you: for whom he hath sent, him ye believe not.
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life.
I receive not honour from men.
But I know you, that ye have not the love of God in you.
I am come in my Father’s name, and ye receive me not: if another shall come in his own name, him ye will receive.
How can ye believe, which receive honour one of another, and seek not the honour that cometh from God only?
Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father: there is one that accuseth you, even Moses, in whom ye trust.
For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me.
But if ye believe not his writings, how shall ye believe my words?

chapters.summary: At "a feast of the Jews" Jesus goes up to Jerusalem and comes to the pool called Bethesda, "having five porches," where "a great multitude of impotent folk, of blind, halt, withered" lie waiting "for the moving of the water." Finding a man sick "thirty and eight years," he asks, "Wilt thou be made whole?" and, hearing only the man's account of never reaching the water first, commands, "Rise, take up thy bed, and walk." The healing is "immediately" done, but it is the sabbath, and the authorities protest that carrying a bed "is not lawful." Jesus finds him later in the temple with a warning: "sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee." Persecuted for the sabbath work, Jesus answers, "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work," and the charge sharpens: he is "making himself equal with God." The rest of the chapter is his defense. The Son "can do nothing of himself," yet does whatever the Father does; the Father "hath committed all judgment unto the Son," "that all men should honour the Son, even as they honour the Father." Whoever hears and believes "is passed from death unto life," and an hour comes when "all that are in the graves shall hear his voice." He then calls his witnesses: John, "a burning and a shining light"; the works given him "to finish"; the Father himself; and the Scriptures, for "they are they which testify of me." Yet "ye will not come to me, that ye might have life," though even Moses "wrote of me."
takeaways: The offense in this chapter is not the healing but the claim behind it: by calling God his own Father and his own work continuous with the Father's, Jesus is heard, correctly, as "making himself equal with God."
Both life and judgment are handed over to the Son, so that honoring or refusing him is honoring or refusing the Father who sent him; there is no reverence for God that bypasses Christ.
Eternal life begins now in hearing and believing—the believer already "is passed from death unto life"—while still awaiting the hour when the dead come bodily out of the graves at his voice.
Scripture searched apart from coming to Christ becomes a substitute for him; the texts themselves "testify of me" and are meant to end in a person, not in study.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 20:8-11 — the sabbath commandment
crossRefs.why: The command to "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy" and to do no work upon it is the law invoked against the healed man and against Jesus. Read alongside, it shows the real dispute is not about rest but about who holds authority over the sabbath, since Jesus answers by claiming the Father's own unceasing work as his own.

crossRefs.label: Daniel 7:13-14 — one like the Son of man given everlasting dominion
crossRefs.why: Daniel sees "one like the Son of man" brought before the Ancient of days and given a kingdom that "shall not pass away." Jesus' statement that the Father "hath given him authority to execute judgment also, because he is the Son of man" draws on this vision, grounding his claim to judge in a prophecy his hearers already knew.

crossRefs.label: Deuteronomy 19:15 — a matter established by two or three witnesses
crossRefs.why: The law refuses to let a charge stand on a single witness, requiring two or three to establish any matter. Jesus' catalogue of witnesses—John, his works, the Father, the Scriptures—answers that legal standard directly, following his own concession that "If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true."

crossRefs.label: Deuteronomy 18:15-19 — the promise of a prophet like Moses
crossRefs.why: Moses promises that God will raise up a prophet from among the people whose words must be heard. Jesus' closing charge that Moses "wrote of me," and that disbelief in Moses' writings blocks belief in his own words, points to promises of this kind as the hinge of the argument.

crossRefs.label: John 9:1-16 — the man born blind healed on the sabbath
crossRefs.why: John narrates a second sabbath healing that provokes the same accusation and then a formal interrogation of the man who was cured. The pairing shows how consistently Jesus' sabbath works became the occasion on which people were forced to decide who he is.

interpretationNotes.claim: Jesus' words to the healed man in the temple, "Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee," are read in the Catholic tradition as showing that bodily healing is ordered toward the deeper healing of the soul—part of a consistent pattern in which Christ joins the forgiveness of sin to his restoring work, a pattern the Church sees carried forward in her care of the sick and of penitents.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the warning as a direct pastoral call to repentance rather than as the seed of a sacramental system, and many caution against inferring that this man's thirty-eight years of infirmity were punishment for particular sins. Both traditions agree that Jesus is more concerned with the man's standing before God than with his legs, and that the healing is meant to lead him into faith and a changed life.

interpretationNotes.claim: The twofold outcome named here—"they that have done good, unto the resurrection of life; and they that have done evil, unto the resurrection of damnation"—is read in the Catholic tradition as teaching that the final judgment genuinely takes account of a life's deeds, not as a rival to faith but as faith's fruit, so that grace received now must be lived out and can still be refused.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally emphasize the earlier promise that the one who hears and believes already "is passed from death unto life," and read the mention of good and evil deeds as the evidence by which a real faith is recognized rather than as its basis. Differences remain over how present grace and final judgment relate, but both traditions confess a bodily resurrection of all the dead and a final accounting before Christ, and both deny that anyone earns life apart from him.

verses.text: After these things Jesus went over the sea of Galilee, which is the sea of Tiberias.
And a great multitude followed him, because they saw his miracles which he did on them that were diseased.
And Jesus went up into a mountain, and there he sat with his disciples.
And the passover, a feast of the Jews, was nigh.
When Jesus then lifted up his eyes, and saw a great company come unto him, he saith unto Philip, Whence shall we buy bread, that these may eat?
And this he said to prove him: for he himself knew what he would do.
Philip answered him, Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little.
One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, saith unto him,
There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?
And Jesus said, Make the men sit down. Now there was much grass in the place. So the men sat down, in number about five thousand.
And Jesus took the loaves; and when he had given thanks, he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to them that were set down; and likewise of the fishes as much as they would.
When they were filled, he said unto his disciples, Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost.
Therefore they gathered them together, and filled twelve baskets with the fragments of the five barley loaves, which remained over and above unto them that had eaten.
Then those men, when they had seen the miracle that Jesus did, said, This is of a truth that prophet that should come into the world.
When Jesus therefore perceived that they would come and take him by force, to make him a king, he departed again into a mountain himself alone.
And when even was now come, his disciples went down unto the sea,
And entered into a ship, and went over the sea toward Capernaum. And it was now dark, and Jesus was not come to them.
And the sea arose by reason of a great wind that blew.
So when they had rowed about five and twenty or thirty furlongs, they see Jesus walking on the sea, and drawing nigh unto the ship: and they were afraid.
But he saith unto them, It is I; be not afraid.
Then they willingly received him into the ship: and immediately the ship was at the land whither they went.

The day following, when the people which stood on the other side of the sea saw that there was none other boat there, save that one whereinto his disciples were entered, and that Jesus went not with his disciples into the boat, but that his disciples were gone away alone;
( Howbeit there came other boats from Tiberias nigh unto the place where they did eat bread, after that the Lord had given thanks:)
When the people therefore saw that Jesus was not there, neither his disciples, they also took shipping, and came to Capernaum, seeking for Jesus.
And when they had found him on the other side of the sea, they said unto him, Rabbi, when camest thou hither?
Jesus answered them and said, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Ye seek me, not because ye saw the miracles, but because ye did eat of the loaves, and were filled.
Labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life, which the Son of man shall give unto you: for him hath God the Father sealed.
Then said they unto him, What shall we do, that we might work the works of God?
Jesus answered and said unto them, This is the work of God, that ye believe on him whom he hath sent.
They said therefore unto him, What sign shewest thou then, that we may see, and believe thee? what dost thou work?
Our fathers did eat manna in the desert; as it is written, He gave them bread from heaven to eat.
Then Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Moses gave you not that bread from heaven; but my Father giveth you the true bread from heaven.
For the bread of God is he which cometh down from heaven, and giveth life unto the world.
Then said they unto him, Lord, evermore give us this bread.
And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
But I said unto you, That ye also have seen me, and believe not.
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
For I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me.
And this is the Father’s will which hath sent me, that of all which he hath given me I should lose nothing, but should raise it up again at the last day.
And this is the will of him that sent me, that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life: and I will raise him up at the last day.
The Jews then murmured at him, because he said, I am the bread which came down from heaven.
And they said, Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? how is it then that he saith, I came down from heaven?
Jesus therefore answered and said unto them, Murmur not among yourselves.
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
It is written in the prophets, And they shall be all taught of God. Every man therefore that hath heard, and hath learned of the Father, cometh unto me.
Not that any man hath seen the Father, save he which is of God, he hath seen the Father.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me hath everlasting life.
I am that bread of life.
Your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead.
This is the bread which cometh down from heaven, that a man may eat thereof, and not die.
I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world.
The Jews therefore strove among themselves, saying, How can this man give us his flesh to eat?
Then Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you.
Whoso eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day.
For my flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed.
He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him.
As the living Father hath sent me, and I live by the Father: so he that eateth me, even he shall live by me.
This is that bread which came down from heaven: not as your fathers did eat manna, and are dead: he that eateth of this bread shall live for ever.
These things said he in the synagogue, as he taught in Capernaum.
Many therefore of his disciples, when they had heard this, said, This is an hard saying; who can hear it?
When Jesus knew in himself that his disciples murmured at it, he said unto them, Doth this offend you?
What and if ye shall see the Son of man ascend up where he was before?
It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.
But there are some of you that believe not. For Jesus knew from the beginning who they were that believed not, and who should betray him.
And he said, Therefore said I unto you, that no man can come unto me, except it were given unto him of my Father.
From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him.
Then said Jesus unto the twelve, Will ye also go away?
Then Simon Peter answered him, Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life.
And we believe and are sure that thou art that Christ, the Son of the living God.
Jesus answered them, Have not I chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?
He spake of Judas Iscariot the son of Simon: for he it was that should betray him, being one of the twelve.

chapters.summary: Jesus crosses the sea of Galilee near passover and a great multitude follows him for his miracles. Testing Philip—"Whence shall we buy bread, that these may eat?"—he takes a lad's "five barley loaves, and two small fishes," gives thanks, and feeds "about five thousand," with twelve baskets of fragments gathered up "that nothing be lost." The crowd declares him "that prophet that should come into the world" and moves to make him king by force, so he withdraws "into a mountain himself alone." That night the disciples row into a great wind and see him walking on the sea: "It is I; be not afraid." At Capernaum the crowd finds him, and he names their appetite: "Ye seek me, not because ye saw the miracles, but because ye did eat of the loaves, and were filled." Asked for a sign like the manna, he answers that "my Father giveth you the true bread from heaven," then declares, "I am the bread of life." All the Father gives him will come, and none will be cast out; he will "raise him up at the last day." Murmuring hardens when he says "the bread that I will give is my flesh," and then, "Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you." Many call it "an hard saying" and "went back, and walked no more with him." Asked whether the twelve will also go, Peter answers, "Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life."
takeaways: The feeding is a sign before it is a mercy: the crowd is satisfied with bread and misses that the giver is himself the gift, "the bread of life" who alone ends hunger and thirst.

Faith is named as the one work God asks—"that ye believe on him whom he hath sent"—and yet coming to Christ is itself a drawing by the Father, so that grace and response are held together rather than set against each other.
Jesus escalates rather than softens the hard saying about eating his flesh and drinking his blood, and accepts the loss of many disciples rather than qualify it; the offense is deliberate.
Peter's confession shows what faith looks like when understanding runs out: not comprehension, but the conviction that there is nowhere else to go because "thou hast the words of eternal life."

crossRefs.label: Exodus 16:1-15 — manna given in the wilderness
crossRefs.why: Israel murmurs in the desert and God promises, "I will rain bread from heaven for you," to be gathered daily as a test of obedience. The crowd cites this precedent to demand a comparable sign, and Jesus answers that the manna was never the true bread, since "your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead."

crossRefs.label: Psalm 78:23-25 — he rained down manna and gave them corn of heaven
crossRefs.why: The psalm remembers God opening "the doors of heaven" and feeding his people so that "Man did eat angels’ food." It supplies the scriptural wording behind the crowd's quotation, "He gave them bread from heaven to eat," which Jesus reinterprets as pointing past Moses to himself.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 54:13 — all thy children shall be taught of the LORD
crossRefs.why: Isaiah promises a people instructed directly by God rather than only by human teachers. Jesus cites this to explain why some come to him and others do not: "Every man therefore that hath heard, and hath learned of the Father, cometh unto me."

crossRefs.label: Matthew 26:26-28 — Jesus takes bread and the cup at the last supper
crossRefs.why: At the passover meal Jesus takes bread and says "this is my body," and the cup, "this is my blood of the new testament." John records no institution account at the supper, so this scene supplies the setting toward which the language of John 6 is pointed.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 11:23-29 — the Lord's supper and discerning the Lord's body
crossRefs.why: Paul hands on the words "this is my body" as received tradition and warns that eating and drinking "unworthily" makes one "guilty of the body and blood of the Lord." Read alongside John 6, it shows the earliest churches treating the bread and cup as a real participation with real consequences.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition this discourse is read as Jesus' own teaching on the Eucharist. When the hearers object, "How can this man give us his flesh to eat?" he does not retreat into figure but presses further—"my flesh is meat indeed, and my blood is drink indeed"—and ties eating and drinking both to eternal life and to mutual indwelling, "dwelleth in me, and I in him." That he lets the offense stand, and lets many disciples leave rather than explain the words away, is taken as evidence that he means a real eating of his true body and blood, given sacramentally.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the chapter first as teaching about faith, noting that Jesus defines the work of God as believing, promises everlasting life to "He that believeth on me" in the same terms he uses of eating, and concludes that "It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life"—which many take as the key to the whole discourse. Some Protestant traditions still affirm a real spiritual feeding on Christ in the supper, while others read the eating as wholly figurative for faith. Both traditions confess that Christ himself, not merely his benefits, is the food of eternal life, and that no one comes to him unless the Father draws.

interpretationNotes.claim: The Father's will "that of all which he hath given me I should lose nothing," set beside the departure of many disciples and a betrayer among the twelve, is read in the Catholic tradition as affirming the absolute priority of grace—"No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him"—without erasing the real freedom by which one who has followed may still go back and walk no more with him.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters in the Reformed stream read the same verses as strong assurance that all whom the Father truly gives to the Son will be kept and raised at the last day, taking the departures as showing that not everyone who followed outwardly had ever been given. Other Protestant traditions stress human responsibility in terms close to the Catholic reading. Both agree that salvation begins in the Father's initiative and that Christ is faithful to everyone the Father has given him.

verses.text: After these things Jesus walked in Galilee: for he would not walk in Jewry, because the Jews sought to kill him.
Now the Jews’ feast of tabernacles was at hand.
His brethren therefore said unto him, Depart hence, and go into Judæa, that thy disciples also may see the works that thou doest.
For there is no man that doeth any thing in secret, and he himself seeketh to be known openly. If thou do these things, shew thyself to the world.
For neither did his brethren believe in him.
Then Jesus said unto them, My time is not yet come: but your time is alway ready.
The world cannot hate you; but me it hateth, because I testify of it, that the works thereof are evil.
Go ye up unto this feast: I go not up yet unto this feast; for my time is not yet full come.
When he had said these words unto them, he abode still in Galilee.
But when his brethren were gone up, then went he also up unto the feast, not openly, but as it were in secret.
Then the Jews sought him at the feast, and said, Where is he?
And there was much murmuring among the people concerning him: for some said, He is a good man: others said, Nay; but he deceiveth the people.
Howbeit no man spake openly of him for fear of the Jews.
Now about the midst of the feast Jesus went up into the temple, and taught.
And the Jews marvelled, saying, How knoweth this man letters, having never learned?
Jesus answered them, and said, My doctrine is not mine, but his that sent me.
If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God, or whether I speak of myself.
He that speaketh of himself seeketh his own glory: but he that seeketh his glory that sent him, the same is true, and no unrighteousness is in him.
Did not Moses give you the law, and yet none of you keepeth the law? Why go ye about to kill me?
The people answered and said, Thou hast a devil: who goeth about to kill thee?
Jesus answered and said unto them, I have done one work, and ye all marvel.
Moses therefore gave unto you circumcision; ( not because it is of Moses, but of the fathers;) and ye on the sabbath day circumcise a man.
If a man on the sabbath day receive circumcision, that the law of Moses should not be broken; are ye angry at me, because I have made a man every whit whole on the sabbath day?
Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.
Then said some of them of Jerusalem, Is not this he, whom they seek to kill?
But, lo, he speaketh boldly, and they say nothing unto him. Do the rulers know indeed that this is the very Christ?
Howbeit we know this man whence he is: but when Christ cometh, no man knoweth whence he is.
Then cried Jesus in the temple as he taught, saying, Ye both know me, and ye know whence I am: and I am not come of myself, but he that sent me is true, whom ye know not.
But I know him: for I am from him, and he hath sent me.
Then they sought to take him: but no man laid hands on him, because his hour was not yet come.
And many of the people believed on him, and said, When Christ cometh, will he do more miracles than these which this man hath done?
The Pharisees heard that the people murmured such things concerning him; and the Pharisees and the chief priests sent officers to take him.
Then said Jesus unto them, Yet a little while am I with you, and then I go unto him that sent me.
Ye shall seek me, and shall not find me: and where I am, thither ye cannot come.
Then said the Jews among themselves, Whither will he go, that we shall not find him? will he go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles, and teach the Gentiles?
What manner of saying is this that he said, Ye shall seek me, and shall not find me: and where I am, thither ye cannot come?
In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink.
He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.
( But this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive: for the Holy Ghost was not yet given; because that Jesus was not yet glorified.)
Many of the people therefore, when they heard this saying, said, Of a truth this is the Prophet.
Others said, This is the Christ. But some said, Shall Christ come out of Galilee?
Hath not the scripture said, That Christ cometh of the seed of David, and out of the town of Bethlehem, where David was?
So there was a division among the people because of him.
And some of them would have taken him; but no man laid hands on him.
Then came the officers to the chief priests and Pharisees; and they said unto them, Why have ye not brought him?
The officers answered, Never man spake like this man.
Then answered them the Pharisees, Are ye also deceived?
Have any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed on him?
But this people who knoweth not the law are cursed.
Nicodemus saith unto them, (he that came to Jesus by night, being one of them,)
Doth our law judge any man, before it hear him, and know what he doeth?
They answered and said unto him, Art thou also of Galilee? Search, and look: for out of Galilee ariseth no prophet.
And every man went unto his own house.

chapters.summary: Jesus stays in Galilee "because the Jews sought to kill him," and his brethren—of whom John notes, "neither did his brethren believe in him"—press him to go up to the feast of tabernacles and "shew thyself to the world." He answers, "My time is not yet come: but your time is alway ready," then goes up "not openly, but as it were in secret." Midway through the feast he teaches in the temple and the crowds marvel, "How knoweth this man letters, having never learned?" His doctrine, he says, "is not mine, but his that sent me," and can be tested by anyone willing to do God's will. Pressing the sabbath quarrel, he notes that circumcision is performed on the sabbath and asks why they are angry that he "made a man every whit whole on the sabbath day": "Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment." The city divides—some ask whether he is "the very Christ," others object that no one should know where Christ comes from—and though officers are sent to arrest him, "no man laid hands on him, because his hour was not yet come." On "the last day, that great day of the feast" he cries, "If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink," promising that "out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water"—spoken, John explains, "of the Spirit," not yet given "because that Jesus was not yet glorified." The dispute closes with the officers confessing, "Never man spake like this man," Nicodemus pleading for a hearing, and "every man went unto his own house."
takeaways: John shows belief and unbelief forming around the very same words and works; the recurring "division among the people because of him" is the chapter's subject, not its background.
Jesus offers a test anyone can run: "If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine." Willingness to obey precedes the ability to recognize whether teaching is from God.
His life is governed by an hour not yet come, so that neither his brethren's urging nor his enemies' plotting can advance or delay the timing of his glory.
The promise of "rivers of living water" ties the gift of the Spirit to the cross and glorification of Jesus; the Spirit is poured out from a finished work, never apart from it.

crossRefs.label: Leviticus 23:33-43 — the feast of tabernacles
crossRefs.why: The law appoints seven days of dwelling in booths and rejoicing before the LORD at the end of harvest, the feast during which this entire chapter unfolds. Knowing the shape of the feast sharpens why Jesus waits until "the last day, that great day" to cry out about thirst and living water.

crossRefs.label: Zechariah 14:8-9 — living waters going out from Jerusalem
crossRefs.why: Zechariah promises that in that day "living waters shall go out from Jerusalem," in a passage that goes on to picture the nations coming up to keep the feast of tabernacles. Standing in Jerusalem at that very feast, Jesus makes himself the source of those waters, claiming the prophecy for his own person.

crossRefs.label: Ezekiel 47:1-12 — waters issuing from the temple, healing all they touch
crossRefs.why: Ezekiel sees a river flowing out from under the threshold of the house, deepening as it goes, so that "every thing shall live whither the river cometh." Jesus' promise that rivers will flow "out of his belly" identifies him, and then the believer, as the temple from which that life-giving water proceeds.

crossRefs.label: Micah 5:2 — out of Bethlehem shall come forth the ruler of Israel
crossRefs.why: Micah names Bethlehem as the birthplace of a ruler "whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting." The crowd quotes this text to dismiss Jesus as a Galilean, unaware that it fits him precisely, an irony John records without stopping to explain.

crossRefs.label: Acts 2:1-4 — the Spirit poured out at Pentecost
crossRefs.why: Luke narrates the Spirit filling the disciples after Jesus has been raised and exalted, a gift Peter attributes to the ascended Christ having "received of the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost." It is the fulfilment of John's parenthesis that the Spirit "was not yet given; because that Jesus was not yet glorified."

interpretationNotes.claim: Jesus' test, "If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine," is read in the Catholic tradition as evidence that faith is never a purely intellectual verdict but grows through obedience and practice—which is why the tradition treats the whole life of the Church, its worship, sacraments, and moral formation, as the school in which the truth of Christ's teaching becomes recognizable.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally agree that obedience clarifies rather than earns understanding, while stressing that the illumination is the Spirit's work through the word rather than something conferred by ecclesial practice. Both traditions hold that a heart unwilling to do God's will cannot judge Christ's teaching fairly, and that knowledge of God is never merely academic.

interpretationNotes.claim: The "brethren" of Jesus who urge him to go up to the feast are understood in the Catholic tradition as kinsmen—cousins or near relations—rather than as other children of Mary, in keeping with the Church's confession of her perpetual virginity; the biblical vocabulary for family ties is broad enough to carry that wider sense.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally take the word in its ordinary sense and understand these to be younger sons born to Joseph and Mary after Jesus. Both traditions agree on what the passage actually reports about them: that those closest to Jesus by family did not yet believe in him, and that his mission was never underwritten by the approval of his own household.
