verses.text: Jesus went unto the mount of Olives.
And early in the morning he came again into the temple, and all the people came unto him; and he sat down, and taught them.
And the scribes and Pharisees brought unto him a woman taken in adultery; and when they had set her in the midst,
They say unto him, Master, this woman was taken in adultery, in the very act.
Now Moses in the law commanded us, that such should be stoned: but what sayest thou?
This they said, tempting him, that they might have to accuse him. But Jesus stooped down, and with his finger wrote on the ground, as though he heard them not.
So when they continued asking him, he lifted up himself, and said unto them, He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.
And again he stooped down, and wrote on the ground.
And they which heard it, being convicted by their own conscience, went out one by one, beginning at the eldest, even unto the last: and Jesus was left alone, and the woman standing in the midst.
When Jesus had lifted up himself, and saw none but the woman, he said unto her, Woman, where are those thine accusers? hath no man condemned thee?
She said, No man, Lord. And Jesus said unto her, Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.
Then spake Jesus again unto them, saying, I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.
The Pharisees therefore said unto him, Thou bearest record of thyself; thy record is not true.
Jesus answered and said unto them, Though I bear record of myself, yet my record is true: for I know whence I came, and whither I go; but ye cannot tell whence I come, and whither I go.
Ye judge after the flesh; I judge no man.
And yet if I judge, my judgment is true: for I am not alone, but I and the Father that sent me.
It is also written in your law, that the testimony of two men is true.
I am one that bear witness of myself, and the Father that sent me beareth witness of me.
Then said they unto him, Where is thy Father? Jesus answered, Ye neither know me, nor my Father: if ye had known me, ye should have known my Father also.
These words spake Jesus in the treasury, as he taught in the temple: and no man laid hands on him; for his hour was not yet come.
Then said Jesus again unto them, I go my way, and ye shall seek me, and shall die in your sins: whither I go, ye cannot come.
Then said the Jews, Will he kill himself? because he saith, Whither I go, ye cannot come.
And he said unto them, Ye are from beneath; I am from above: ye are of this world; I am not of this world.
I said therefore unto you, that ye shall die in your sins: for if ye believe not that I am he, ye shall die in your sins.
Then said they unto him, Who art thou? And Jesus saith unto them, Even the same that I said unto you from the beginning.
I have many things to say and to judge of you: but he that sent me is true; and I speak to the world those things which I have heard of him.
They understood not that he spake to them of the Father.
Then said Jesus unto them, When ye have lifted up the Son of man, then shall ye know that I am he, and that I do nothing of myself; but as my Father hath taught me, I speak these things.
And he that sent me is with me: the Father hath not left me alone; for I do always those things that please him.
As he spake these words, many believed on him.
Then said Jesus to those Jews which believed on him, If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed;
And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.
They answered him, We be Abraham’s seed, and were never in bondage to any man: how sayest thou, Ye shall be made free?
Jesus answered them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.
And the servant abideth not in the house for ever: but the Son abideth ever.
If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.
I know that ye are Abraham’s seed; but ye seek to kill me, because my word hath no place in you.
I speak that which I have seen with my Father: and ye do that which ye have seen with your father.
They answered and said unto him, Abraham is our father. Jesus saith unto them, If ye were Abraham’s children, ye would do the works of Abraham.
But now ye seek to kill me, a man that hath told you the truth, which I have heard of God: this did not Abraham.
Ye do the deeds of your father. Then said they to him, We be not born of fornication; we have one Father, even God.
Jesus said unto them, If God were your Father, ye would love me: for I proceeded forth and came from God; neither came I of myself, but he sent me.
Why do ye not understand my speech? even because ye cannot hear my word.

Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do. He was a murderer from the beginning, and abode not in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it.
And because I tell you the truth, ye believe me not.
Which of you convinceth me of sin? And if I say the truth, why do ye not believe me?
He that is of God heareth God’s words: ye therefore hear them not, because ye are not of God.
Then answered the Jews, and said unto him, Say we not well that thou art a Samaritan, and hast a devil?
Jesus answered, I have not a devil; but I honour my Father, and ye do dishonour me.
And I seek not mine own glory: there is one that seeketh and judgeth.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, If a man keep my saying, he shall never see death.
Then said the Jews unto him, Now we know that thou hast a devil. Abraham is dead, and the prophets; and thou sayest, If a man keep my saying, he shall never taste of death.
Art thou greater than our father Abraham, which is dead? and the prophets are dead: whom makest thou thyself?
Jesus answered, If I honour myself, my honour is nothing: it is my Father that honoureth me; of whom ye say, that he is your God:
Yet ye have not known him; but I know him: and if I should say, I know him not, I shall be a liar like unto you: but I know him, and keep his saying.
Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day: and he saw it, and was glad.
Then said the Jews unto him, Thou art not yet fifty years old, and hast thou seen Abraham?
Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Before Abraham was, I am.
Then took they up stones to cast at him: but Jesus hid himself, and went out of the temple, going through the midst of them, and so passed by.

chapters.summary: From the mount of Olives Jesus returns at daybreak to teach in the temple, where scribes and Pharisees set before him a woman "taken in adultery, in the very act," citing Moses' penalty of stoning and "tempting him, that they might have to accuse him." He stoops and writes "on the ground, as though he heard them not," then answers, "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her." The accusers withdraw "one by one, beginning at the eldest," and he tells her, "Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." (Many of the earliest surviving copies of John lack this episode or place it elsewhere, though the Church has long received and read it as Scripture.) Jesus then declares, "I am the light of the world," and a long dispute over testimony follows: his record stands because "I am not alone, but I and the Father that sent me." He warns that they will "die in your sins" unless they believe, and that "when ye have lifted up the Son of man, then shall ye know that I am he." To those who believe he promises, "ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free"—freedom not from any earthly power but from sin, since "Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin." Against the appeal to descent he distinguishes lineage from likeness: "If ye were Abraham’s children, ye would do the works of Abraham." It ends in the sharpest claim of all, "Before Abraham was, I am," at which stones are taken up and "Jesus hid himself, and went out of the temple."
takeaways: Mercy and moral seriousness are not rivals: Jesus refuses to condemn the woman and in the same breath tells her to "go, and sin no more," neither denying the sin nor leaving her in it.
The trap collapses because no one present qualifies to throw the first stone; it is conscience rather than argument that empties the courtyard, "beginning at the eldest."
Freedom in this chapter is neither political nor ancestral but release from the servitude of sin, granted by the Son who "abideth ever" in the household and can therefore make others free "indeed."
"Before Abraham was, I am" claims divine existence and not merely priority in time, which is why the response is stones rather than further debate.

crossRefs.label: Deuteronomy 17:6-7 — the hands of the witnesses first upon the condemned
crossRefs.why: The law requires two or three witnesses for a capital sentence and puts "The hands of the witnesses" first in carrying it out. Jesus' words about the one "without sin" casting the first stone turn that provision directly back on the accusers, who are acting as the witnesses in the case.

crossRefs.label: Leviticus 20:10 — the penalty for adultery falls on both parties
crossRefs.why: The law condemns "the adulterer and the adulteress" alike, and Deuteronomy likewise requires that both die. Since only the woman is brought forward, the appeal to Moses is already selective, exposing the aim as accusation of Jesus rather than justice for the offense.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 9:1-2 — the people that walked in darkness have seen a great light
crossRefs.why: Isaiah promises light dawning on those who "dwell in the land of the shadow of death," beginning in the despised northern territory. Jesus' claim to be "the light of the world," with the promise that his follower "shall not walk in darkness," answers that prophecy in the first person.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 3:13-15 — God reveals his name as I AM THAT I AM
crossRefs.why: God gives Moses the name "I AM THAT I AM" as the name by which he is to be identified to Israel. Jesus' repeated "I am he" and finally "Before Abraham was, I am" take up that name, which accounts for the immediate attempt to stone him.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 22:15-18 — in thy seed shall all the nations be blessed
crossRefs.why: On the mountain of sacrifice God swears to Abraham that "in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed." Jesus' claim that Abraham "rejoiced to see my day: and he saw it, and was glad" points to promises of this kind, glimpsed by Abraham from far off and fulfilled in the one now standing in the temple.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the encounter with the woman taken in adultery is read as the pattern of sacramental mercy: Christ, the one person present with standing to condemn, absolves without excusing, and sends the forgiven sinner away under a command—"go, and sin no more"—so that absolution and amendment of life belong together. The Church has kept the passage as Scripture and read it as a charter for the ministry of reconciliation, while acknowledging that its place in the manuscript tradition of John is unusual.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the scene as a display of Christ's own authority to forgive and as a rebuke to self-righteous judgment, without deriving from it a priestly power of absolution exercised by others. Many also treat the passage's textual history more cautiously, some bracketing it in print while still preaching it. Both traditions agree that the words are wholly consistent with everything else Jesus says and does, and that his mercy neither denies the sin nor abandons the sinner to it.

interpretationNotes.claim: Jesus' distinction between Abraham's seed and Abraham's children—"If ye were Abraham’s children, ye would do the works of Abraham"—is read in the Catholic tradition as showing that inherited membership never substitutes for a living faith that acts, so that belonging to the household of God is a matter of continuing in Christ's word rather than of standing alone.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally reach the same conclusion by a different accent, arguing that true descent from Abraham is by faith rather than by works, and reading the "works of Abraham" as the evidence of that faith rather than its ground. Both traditions agree that no lineage, ancestry, or affiliation secures anyone apart from believing and abiding in the word of Christ.

verses.text: And as Jesus passed by, he saw a man which was blind from his birth.
And his disciples asked him, saying, Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?
Jesus answered, Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him.
I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work.
As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.
When he had thus spoken, he spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay,
And said unto him, Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, ( which is by interpretation, Sent.) He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing.
The neighbours therefore, and they which before had seen him that he was blind, said, Is not this he that sat and begged?
Some said, This is he: others said, He is like him: but he said, I am he.
Therefore said they unto him, How were thine eyes opened?
He answered and said, A man that is called Jesus made clay, and anointed mine eyes, and said unto me, Go to the pool of Siloam, and wash: and I went and washed, and I received sight.
Then said they unto him, Where is he? He said, I know not.
They brought to the Pharisees him that aforetime was blind.
And it was the sabbath day when Jesus made the clay, and opened his eyes.
Then again the Pharisees also asked him how he had received his sight. He said unto them, He put clay upon mine eyes, and I washed, and do see.

Therefore said some of the Pharisees, This man is not of God, because he keepeth not the sabbath day. Others said, How can a man that is a sinner do such miracles? And there was a division among them.
They say unto the blind man again, What sayest thou of him, that he hath opened thine eyes? He said, He is a prophet.
But the Jews did not believe concerning him, that he had been blind, and received his sight, until they called the parents of him that had received his sight.
And they asked them, saying, Is this your son, who ye say was born blind? how then doth he now see?
His parents answered them and said, We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind:
But by what means he now seeth, we know not; or who hath opened his eyes, we know not: he is of age; ask him: he shall speak for himself.
These words spake his parents, because they feared the Jews: for the Jews had agreed already, that if any man did confess that he was Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue.
Therefore said his parents, He is of age; ask him.
Then again called they the man that was blind, and said unto him, Give God the praise: we know that this man is a sinner.
He answered and said, Whether he be a sinner or no, I know not: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see.
Then said they to him again, What did he to thee? how opened he thine eyes?
He answered them, I have told you already, and ye did not hear: wherefore would ye hear it again? will ye also be his disciples?
Then they reviled him, and said, Thou art his disciple; but we are Moses’ disciples.
We know that God spake unto Moses: as for this fellow, we know not from whence he is.
The man answered and said unto them, Why herein is a marvellous thing, that ye know not from whence he is, and yet he hath opened mine eyes.
Now we know that God heareth not sinners: but if any man be a worshipper of God, and doeth his will, him he heareth.
Since the world began was it not heard that any man opened the eyes of one that was born blind.
If this man were not of God, he could do nothing.
They answered and said unto him, Thou wast altogether born in sins, and dost thou teach us? And they cast him out.
Jesus heard that they had cast him out; and when he had found him, he said unto him, Dost thou believe on the Son of God?
He answered and said, Who is he, Lord, that I might believe on him?
And Jesus said unto him, Thou hast both seen him, and it is he that talketh with thee.
And he said, Lord, I believe. And he worshipped him.
And Jesus said, For judgment I am come into this world, that they which see not might see; and that they which see might be made blind.
And some of the Pharisees which were with him heard these words, and said unto him, Are we blind also?
Jesus said unto them, If ye were blind, ye should have no sin: but now ye say, We see; therefore your sin remaineth.

chapters.summary: Passing by, Jesus sees "a man which was blind from his birth," and the disciples ask whose sin caused it. Jesus refuses the accounting—"Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents"—and turns the question from cause to purpose, "that the works of God should be made manifest in him," adding, "I am the light of the world." He spits on the ground, makes clay, anoints the man's eyes, and sends him to wash in the pool of Siloam, "which is by interpretation, Sent"; the man "came seeing." Because "it was the sabbath day when Jesus made the clay," the Pharisees interrogate him and split: some say "This man is not of God," others ask, "How can a man that is a sinner do such miracles?" The man's witness grows bolder under pressure—first "He is a prophet," then "one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see," then a rebuke of his judges, "yet he hath opened mine eyes." His parents, fearing expulsion from the synagogue, deflect: "he is of age; ask him." The leaders "cast him out," and Jesus seeks him: "Dost thou believe on the Son of God?" He answers, "Lord, I believe. And he worshipped him." Jesus closes with the reversal: he came "that they which see not might see; and that they which see might be made blind," and to those who say "We see," "your sin remaineth."
takeaways: Jesus rejects reading affliction as a ledger of personal guilt, redirecting the disciples from the question of blame to the purpose God will work through it.
Faith here is a growing thing: the man moves from reporting a bare fact, to calling Jesus "a prophet," to confessing him and worshipping—each step taken under mounting pressure.
Sight and blindness are inverted. The one who admits he cannot see receives sight; those confident that they already see are the ones left in their sin.
Confessing Christ costs something real—expulsion from the synagogue—and it is precisely the man cast out whom Jesus goes to find.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 35:5-6 — then the eyes of the blind shall be opened
crossRefs.why: Isaiah promises that when God comes to save, the eyes of the blind will be opened and the lame will leap. Read beside John 9, the healing is not merely a kindness but a signed claim that the promised age of God's coming has arrived in Jesus.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 42:6-7 — a light of the Gentiles, to open the blind eyes
crossRefs.why: The servant is given as a covenant and "a light of the Gentiles," commissioned to open blind eyes and free those who sit in darkness. The pairing explains why Jesus announces himself as "the light of the world" in the very act of opening a blind man's eyes.

crossRefs.label: John 8:12 — I am the light of the world
crossRefs.why: Immediately before this chapter Jesus makes the same claim and promises that whoever follows him "shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life." John 9 then enacts the saying, so that the words and the sign interpret each other.

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 4:3-6 — blinded minds and the light shining in our hearts
crossRefs.why: Paul describes unbelief as a blindness of the mind and conversion as God shining light into the heart, giving "the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ." Alongside John 9 it names the deeper blindness the chapter exposes in those who insist they can see.

crossRefs.label: Ephesians 5:8-14 — ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord
crossRefs.why: Paul frames the Christian life as a passage from darkness into light with a call to walk as "children of light," closing with a summons to awake so that "Christ shall give thee light." The passage draws out the moral shape of what the healed man receives: not only sight, but a new way of walking.

interpretationNotes.claim: The pattern of the healing—an anointing with clay followed by washing in the pool called "Sent," issuing in the confession "Lord, I believe"—is read in the Catholic tradition as an image of baptism, in which anointing and water open the eyes of the soul and bring a person to faith and worship.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the clay and the pool as elements of a sign whose meaning is chiefly Christological rather than sacramental: Jesus is the light of the world, and the man's obedience to his word is what leads to sight. They emphasize that faith is the means by which anyone is enlightened, cautioning against reading a later sacramental rite back into the narrative. Both traditions hold that the man's sight is entirely God's gift and not his achievement, and that the chapter moves deliberately from physical healing to worship of Christ.

interpretationNotes.claim: Jesus' answer that the blindness came "neither" from the man's sin nor his parents', but so "that the works of God should be made manifest in him," is read in the Catholic tradition as denying any simple equation of suffering with punishment, while holding that God permits an evil only because he can order it to a greater good.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readers likewise reject the disciples' assumption that the blindness must be someone's fault, and many stress even more strongly that God's sovereign purpose, not human merit or demerit, governs the man's condition from birth. Some resist any language of God merely permitting the affliction, preferring to speak of his direct ordination of it for his glory. Both traditions agree that the text forbids using another person's suffering as evidence of their guilt, and that God's purpose in it is revealed only in Christ's work.

verses.text: Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber.
But he that entereth in by the door is the shepherd of the sheep.
To him the porter openeth; and the sheep hear his voice: and he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out.
And when he putteth forth his own sheep, he goeth before them, and the sheep follow him: for they know his voice.
And a stranger will they not follow, but will flee from him: for they know not the voice of strangers.
This parable spake Jesus unto them: but they understood not what things they were which he spake unto them.
Then said Jesus unto them again, Verily, verily, I say unto you, I am the door of the sheep.
All that ever came before me are thieves and robbers: but the sheep did not hear them.
I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture.
The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.
I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep.
The hireling fleeth, because he is an hireling, and careth not for the sheep.
I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine.
As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep.
And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.
Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again.
No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. This commandment have I received of my Father.
There was a division therefore again among the Jews for these sayings.
And many of them said, He hath a devil, and is mad; why hear ye him?
Others said, These are not the words of him that hath a devil. Can a devil open the eyes of the blind?
And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter.
And Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon’s porch.
Then came the Jews round about him, and said unto him, How long dost thou make us to doubt? If thou be the Christ, tell us plainly.
Jesus answered them, I told you, and ye believed not: the works that I do in my Father’s name, they bear witness of me.
But ye believe not, because ye are not of my sheep, as I said unto you.
My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me:
And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.
My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all; and no man is able to pluck them out of my Father’s hand.
I and my Father are one.
Then the Jews took up stones again to stone him.
Jesus answered them, Many good works have I shewed you from my Father; for which of those works do ye stone me?
The Jews answered him, saying, For a good work we stone thee not; but for blasphemy; and because that thou, being a man, makest thyself God.
Jesus answered them, Is it not written in your law, I said, Ye are gods?
If he called them gods, unto whom the word of God came, and the scripture can not be broken;
Say ye of him, whom the Father hath sanctified, and sent into the world, Thou blasphemest; because I said, I am the Son of God?
If I do not the works of my Father, believe me not.
But if I do, though ye believe not me, believe the works: that ye may know, and believe, that the Father is in me, and I in him.
Therefore they sought again to take him: but he escaped out of their hand,
And went away again beyond Jordan into the place where John at first baptized; and there he abode.
And many resorted unto him, and said, John did no miracle: but all things that John spake of this man were true.
And many believed on him there.

chapters.summary: Jesus continues from the healing of the blind man with a figure drawn from the sheepfold: whoever climbs in "some other way" is "a thief and a robber," while the true shepherd enters by the door, "calleth his own sheep by name," and leads them out, and they follow "for they know his voice." When the hearers miss the point, he applies it twice to himself: "I am the door of the sheep," by whom anyone entering "shall be saved," and "I am the good shepherd," who unlike the hireling does not flee the wolf but "giveth his life for the sheep." He knows his own as "the Father knoweth me," speaks of sheep he has "which are not of this fold" and must also bring, so that "there shall be one fold, and one shepherd," and insists his death is freely chosen: "No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself." The crowd divides again, some saying "He hath a devil," others recalling the opened eyes. At the feast of the dedication, in winter, they press him in Solomon's porch: "If thou be the Christ, tell us plainly." He points to his works, promises that "neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand," and says, "I and my Father are one." They take up stones for blasphemy; he answers from their own law, appeals again to his works, escapes their hand, and withdraws beyond Jordan, where "many believed on him."
takeaways: Christ's shepherding is personal and self-sacrificing: he calls his own by name and freely lays down his life, which is what distinguishes him from the hireling who serves only while it is safe.
Belonging to Christ is marked by hearing and following his voice rather than by mere proximity to the fold; recognition of the shepherd is itself the sign of the sheep.
The promise of "one fold, and one shepherd" makes the gathering of those outside the present fold part of Christ's own intention, not an afterthought.
"I and my Father are one" is heard by his opponents as a claim to divinity, and Jesus does not retract it—he defends it by pointing to works that only God could do.

crossRefs.label: Ezekiel 34:11-16 — the LORD himself will search out and feed his flock
crossRefs.why: Against shepherds who fed themselves and scattered the sheep, God declares that he himself will seek out his flock, feed it, and bind up the broken. Read alongside John 10 this makes Jesus' claim to be the good shepherd a claim to be doing what God had reserved to himself.

crossRefs.label: Ezekiel 34:23 — I will set up one shepherd over them
crossRefs.why: The same prophecy promises a single appointed shepherd in the line of David who will feed the flock. It illuminates why Jesus speaks not merely of good shepherding but of "one fold, and one shepherd," the promised single pastor of a reunited people.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 23:1-4 — the LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want
crossRefs.why: The psalm speaks of the LORD leading, feeding, and accompanying his own even through the valley of the shadow of death. It supplies the devotional vocabulary Jesus takes up, and his promise that no one can pluck his sheep from his hand answers the psalm's confidence with a person.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 82:6 — I have said, Ye are gods
crossRefs.why: This is the verse Jesus quotes back at those about to stone him, where human judges entrusted with God's word are addressed in exalted terms. Reading it in place shows the shape of his argument: if Scripture can speak that way of others, the charge of blasphemy cannot rest merely on the words "I am the Son of God."

crossRefs.label: 1 Peter 5:2-4 — feed the flock of God, awaiting the chief Shepherd
crossRefs.why: Peter charges elders to shepherd God's flock willingly rather than for gain, under the coming "chief Shepherd." It shows how the early Church applied John 10 to pastoral office: those who tend the sheep answer to the one shepherd and must not be hirelings.

interpretationNotes.claim: Christ's promise that "there shall be one fold, and one shepherd" is read in the Catholic tradition as Christ's own will for a visible unity of his flock—one communion gathered under his shepherding, which he exercises in history through the pastors he appoints—so that division among Christians is a wound against his expressed intention.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the one flock as the whole company of true believers, united in Christ by faith rather than by a single visible structure, and often take the "other sheep" as the Gentiles brought in alongside Israel. On this reading unity is real but chiefly spiritual, and outward church order may legitimately vary. Both traditions affirm that the unity of Christ's people is his own doing and desire, that it is grounded in hearing his voice, and that Christian division is contrary to his prayer for his own.

interpretationNotes.claim: Jesus' promise that his sheep "shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand" is read in the Catholic tradition as an unshakable assurance about Christ's power to keep his own, while holding that a person can still freely refuse to keep hearing his voice, since the security is located in the shepherd's hand and not in a guarantee that removes human freedom.

counterpoint.summary: Many Protestant interpreters, especially in the Reformed stream, read the same words as a promise that those truly given to Christ by the Father will certainly be preserved to the end, so that no genuine sheep is finally lost. Other Protestants hold a view closer to the Catholic emphasis on continuing faith. Both traditions agree that no external power can wrest a believer from Christ, and that whatever perseverance a Christian has is the gift of the shepherd rather than the strength of the sheep.

verses.text: Now a certain man was sick, named Lazarus, of Bethany, the town of Mary and her sister Martha.
(It was that Mary which anointed the Lord with ointment, and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was sick.)
Therefore his sisters sent unto him, saying, Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick.
When Jesus heard that, he said, This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God might be glorified thereby.
Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus.
When he had heard therefore that he was sick, he abode two days still in the same place where he was.
Then after that saith he to his disciples, Let us go into Judæa again.
His disciples say unto him, Master, the Jews of late sought to stone thee; and goest thou thither again?
Jesus answered, Are there not twelve hours in the day? If any man walk in the day, he stumbleth not, because he seeth the light of this world.
But if a man walk in the night, he stumbleth, because there is no light in him.
These things said he: and after that he saith unto them, Our friend Lazarus sleepeth; but I go, that I may awake him out of sleep.
Then said his disciples, Lord, if he sleep, he shall do well.
Howbeit Jesus spake of his death: but they thought that he had spoken of taking of rest in sleep.
Then said Jesus unto them plainly, Lazarus is dead.
And I am glad for your sakes that I was not there, to the intent ye may believe; nevertheless let us go unto him.
Then said Thomas, which is called Didymus, unto his fellowdisciples, Let us also go, that we may die with him.
Then when Jesus came, he found that he had lain in the grave four days already.
Now Bethany was nigh unto Jerusalem, about fifteen furlongs off:
And many of the Jews came to Martha and Mary, to comfort them concerning their brother.
Then Martha, as soon as she heard that Jesus was coming, went and met him: but Mary sat still in the house.
Then said Martha unto Jesus, Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.
But I know, that even now, whatsoever thou wilt ask of God, God will give it thee.
Jesus saith unto her, Thy brother shall rise again.
Martha saith unto him, I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day.
Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live:
And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this?
She saith unto him, Yea, Lord: I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God, which should come into the world.
And when she had so said, she went her way, and called Mary her sister secretly, saying, The Master is come, and calleth for thee.
As soon as she heard that, she arose quickly, and came unto him.
Now Jesus was not yet come into the town, but was in that place where Martha met him.
The Jews then which were with her in the house, and comforted her, when they saw Mary, that she rose up hastily and went out, followed her, saying, She goeth unto the grave to weep there.
Then when Mary was come where Jesus was, and saw him, she fell down at his feet, saying unto him, Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.
When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews also weeping which came with her, he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled,
And said, Where have ye laid him? They said unto him, Lord, come and see.
Jesus wept.
Then said the Jews, Behold how he loved him!
And some of them said, Could not this man, which opened the eyes of the blind, have caused that even this man should not have died?
Jesus therefore again groaning in himself cometh to the grave. It was a cave, and a stone lay upon it.
Jesus said, Take ye away the stone. Martha, the sister of him that was dead, saith unto him, Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days.
Jesus saith unto her, Said I not unto thee, that, if thou wouldest believe, thou shouldest see the glory of God?
Then they took away the stone from the place where the dead was laid. And Jesus lifted up his eyes, and said, Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me.
And I knew that thou hearest me always: but because of the people which stand by I said it, that they may believe that thou hast sent me.
And when he thus had spoken, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth.
And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go.
Then many of the Jews which came to Mary, and had seen the things which Jesus did, believed on him.
But some of them went their ways to the Pharisees, and told them what things Jesus had done.
Then gathered the chief priests and the Pharisees a council, and said, What do we? for this man doeth many miracles.
If we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him: and the Romans shall come and take away both our place and nation.
And one of them, named Caiaphas, being the high priest that same year, said unto them, Ye know nothing at all,
Nor consider that it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not.
And this spake he not of himself: but being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus should die for that nation;
And not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.
Then from that day forth they took counsel together for to put him to death.
Jesus therefore walked no more openly among the Jews; but went thence unto a country near to the wilderness, into a city called Ephraim, and there continued with his disciples.
And the Jews’ passover was nigh at hand: and many went out of the country up to Jerusalem before the passover, to purify themselves.
Then sought they for Jesus, and spake among themselves, as they stood in the temple, What think ye, that he will not come to the feast?
Now both the chief priests and the Pharisees had given a commandment, that, if any man knew where he were, he should shew it, that they might take him.

chapters.summary: Word comes from Bethany that Lazarus, "he whom thou lovest," is sick. Jesus answers that the sickness is "for the glory of God," then deliberately waits two days before proposing to return to Judaea, where the disciples fear stoning and Thomas resolves, "Let us also go, that we may die with him." Jesus speaks of Lazarus sleeping, then plainly: "Lazarus is dead." He arrives after four days in the grave. Martha meets him with grief and hope—"Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died"—and receives the great self-revelation, "I am the resurrection, and the life," with the question "Believest thou this?" She confesses him "the Christ, the Son of God." Mary falls at his feet with the same lament, and Jesus, seeing the weeping, "groaned in the spirit, and was troubled," and "Jesus wept." At the cave he has the stone taken away despite Martha's protest, gives thanks to the Father aloud "because of the people which stand by," and cries, "Lazarus, come forth." The dead man emerges bound in graveclothes: "Loose him, and let him go." Many believe; others report to the Pharisees, and the council, fearing Rome, hears Caiaphas say that "it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people"—words John reads as unwitting prophecy that Jesus would die to gather "the children of God that were scattered abroad." From that day they plot his death, and he withdraws to Ephraim.
takeaways: Jesus' delay is not indifference but deliberate: the greater sign, and the deeper faith it works, matter more to him than sparing his friends the interval of grief.
"I am the resurrection, and the life" moves hope from a distant event to a person; Martha already believed in a resurrection "at the last day," and is asked to believe in the one standing before her.
Christ's tears and groaning show a real human heart confronting death—he does not console from a distance, and the shortest verse in the Gospel is his grief.

The sign that most clearly displays his power over death is precisely what seals the decision to kill him, and the high priest's political calculation becomes, against his intent, a true statement of the atonement.

crossRefs.label: Ezekiel 37:12-14 — I will open your graves and bring you up
crossRefs.why: God promises to open the graves of his people, raise them, and put his Spirit in them so they shall live. Reading it beside the call of Lazarus from the cave shows Jesus doing in one man, visibly, what the prophet announced for the whole people.

crossRefs.label: Daniel 12:2 — many that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake
crossRefs.why: Daniel gives one of the clearest Old Testament statements of a general resurrection to everlasting life or contempt. It is the hope Martha already holds when she speaks of "the resurrection at the last day," which makes Jesus' reply a claim to be its source.

crossRefs.label: John 5:25-29 — all that are in the graves shall hear his voice
crossRefs.why: Earlier in the same Gospel Jesus says the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God and live, and that all in the graves will finally come forth at his voice. Lazarus emerging at a spoken command is that promise given in advance as a sign.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 15:20-26 — Christ the firstfruits, and death the last enemy destroyed
crossRefs.why: Paul distinguishes Christ's resurrection as the firstfruits from the general resurrection that follows, ending with death itself destroyed. It clarifies what the raising of Lazarus is and is not: a restoration to this life that points forward to a resurrection that will not be undone.

crossRefs.label: Luke 10:38-42 — Martha serving and Mary at Jesus' feet
crossRefs.why: Luke shows the same two sisters in character: Martha busy and forthright, Mary seated at Jesus' feet listening. The portraits carry over here, where Martha goes out to meet and argue with him while Mary falls at his feet in silence and tears.

interpretationNotes.claim: The sisters' appeal on behalf of their brother—sending word to Jesus, and then pleading with him at the grave—is read in the Catholic tradition as a pattern of intercession, in which one person's love and petition are genuinely taken up into Christ's work for another, a logic the tradition extends to asking the friends of God in heaven to pray for us.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the intercession here as living friends appealing directly to Christ, and decline to extend the pattern to petitions addressed to the departed, holding that Scripture directs prayer to God through Christ alone. They stress that what moves the outcome is Jesus' own love and power, not the sisters' merit. Both traditions affirm that Christians should pray for one another, that the sisters' appeal is answered entirely by Christ's authority over death, and that faith in him is what the whole episode is meant to produce.

interpretationNotes.claim: Caiaphas' words, which John says he spoke "not of himself" but "being high priest that year," are read in the Catholic tradition as showing that God can speak truly through a sacred office even when the man holding it acts in bad faith, so that the efficacy of the office is not simply reduced to the holiness of its occupant.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters more often read the scene as dramatic irony under God's sovereignty: God overrules a cynical political calculation to state the truth of the atonement, without this implying any standing authority attached to the priestly office itself. They note John's own gloss supplies the theology, not Caiaphas. Both traditions agree that the sentence is true in a sense its speaker never intended—that one man would die for the people—and that God governs even the plotting of Christ's enemies toward the salvation of the scattered children of God.

verses.text: Then Jesus six days before the passover came to Bethany, where Lazarus was which had been dead, whom he raised from the dead.
There they made him a supper; and Martha served: but Lazarus was one of them that sat at the table with him.
Then took Mary a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly, and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair: and the house was filled with the odour of the ointment.
Then saith one of his disciples, Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, which should betray him,
Why was not this ointment sold for three hundred pence, and given to the poor?
This he said, not that he cared for the poor; but because he was a thief, and had the bag, and bare what was put therein.
Then said Jesus, Let her alone: against the day of my burying hath she kept this.
For the poor always ye have with you; but me ye have not always.
Much people of the Jews therefore knew that he was there: and they came not for Jesus’ sake only, but that they might see Lazarus also, whom he had raised from the dead.
But the chief priests consulted that they might put Lazarus also to death;
Because that by reason of him many of the Jews went away, and believed on Jesus.
On the next day much people that were come to the feast, when they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem,
Took branches of palm trees, and went forth to meet him, and cried, Hosanna: Blessed is the King of Israel that cometh in the name of the Lord.
And Jesus, when he had found a young ass, sat thereon; as it is written,
Fear not, daughter of Sion: behold, thy King cometh, sitting on an ass’s colt.
These things understood not his disciples at the first: but when Jesus was glorified, then remembered they that these things were written of him, and that they had done these things unto him.
The people therefore that was with him when he called Lazarus out of his grave, and raised him from the dead, bare record.
For this cause the people also met him, for that they heard that he had done this miracle.
The Pharisees therefore said among themselves, Perceive ye how ye prevail nothing? behold, the world is gone after him.
And there were certain Greeks among them that came up to worship at the feast:
The same came therefore to Philip, which was of Bethsaida of Galilee, and desired him, saying, Sir, we would see Jesus.
Philip cometh and telleth Andrew: and again Andrew and Philip tell Jesus.
And Jesus answered them, saying, The hour is come, that the Son of man should be glorified.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.
He that loveth his life shall lose it; and he that hateth his life in this world shall keep it unto life eternal.
If any man serve me, let him follow me; and where I am, there shall also my servant be: if any man serve me, him will my Father honour.
Now is my soul troubled; and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour: but for this cause came I unto this hour.
Father, glorify thy name. Then came there a voice from heaven, saying, I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again.
The people therefore, that stood by, and heard it, said that it thundered: others said, An angel spake to him.
Jesus answered and said, This voice came not because of me, but for your sakes.
Now is the judgment of this world: now shall the prince of this world be cast out.
And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me.
This he said, signifying what death he should die.
The people answered him, We have heard out of the law that Christ abideth for ever: and how sayest thou, The Son of man must be lifted up? who is this Son of man?
Then Jesus said unto them, Yet a little while is the light with you. Walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you: for he that walketh in darkness knoweth not whither he goeth.
While ye have light, believe in the light, that ye may be the children of light. These things spake Jesus, and departed, and did hide himself from them.
But though he had done so many miracles before them, yet they believed not on him:
That the saying of Esaias the prophet might be fulfilled, which he spake, Lord, who hath believed our report? and to whom hath the arm of the Lord been revealed?
Therefore they could not believe, because that Esaias said again,
He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart; that they should not see with their eyes, nor understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them.
These things said Esaias, when he saw his glory, and spake of him.
Nevertheless among the chief rulers also many believed on him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, lest they should be put out of the synagogue:
For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.
Jesus cried and said, He that believeth on me, believeth not on me, but on him that sent me.
And he that seeth me seeth him that sent me.
I am come a light into the world, that whosoever believeth on me should not abide in darkness.
And if any man hear my words, and believe not, I judge him not: for I came not to judge the world, but to save the world.
He that rejecteth me, and receiveth not my words, hath one that judgeth him: the word that I have spoken, the same shall judge him in the last day.
For I have not spoken of myself; but the Father which sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.
And I know that his commandment is life everlasting: whatsoever I speak therefore, even as the Father said unto me, so I speak.

chapters.summary: Six days before the passover Jesus returns to Bethany, where Martha serves and the raised Lazarus sits at table. Mary pours "a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly" on his feet and wipes them with her hair, until "the house was filled with the odour of the ointment." Judas objects for the poor, though he "was a thief, and had the bag"; Jesus defends her: "against the day of my burying hath she kept this." Next day the festival crowd takes "branches of palm trees" and cries "Hosanna: Blessed is the King of Israel," and Jesus enters on a colt, fulfilling what the disciples grasped only "when Jesus was glorified." The Pharisees concede that "the world is gone after him." Greeks approach Philip: "Sir, we would see Jesus." Jesus answers, "The hour is come": a corn of wheat must fall into the ground and die to bring forth much fruit, and "He that loveth his life shall lose it." His soul is troubled, yet he prays "Father, glorify thy name," and a voice answers from heaven; he announces the judgment of this world and that "if I be lifted up from the earth," he "will draw all men unto me," then bids them walk while they have the light and hides himself. John accounts for their unbelief from the prophet, notes rulers who would not confess because "they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God," and closes with Jesus' last appeal: to see him is to see the Father who sent him.
takeaways: Mary's extravagant and unrepeatable act of love is defended by Jesus against the calculus of usefulness, and he reads it as preparation for his burial, devotion perceiving the coming cross before the disciples do.

The pattern of fruitfulness is death first: the grain must fall into the ground, and the disciple who clings to his life loses it, so the cross is not only what Christ undergoes but the shape of following him.
"Now is my soul troubled" shows a genuine recoil before death held together with obedience; Jesus does not ask to be spared the hour but asks that the Father's name be glorified in it.
Unbelief before many signs is presented as both judgment and culpable choice: eyes are blinded, and yet rulers withhold confession because human esteem matters more to them than God's.

crossRefs.label: Zechariah 9:9 — behold, thy King cometh, lowly, riding upon an ass
crossRefs.why: Zechariah announces a king coming to Jerusalem just, bringing salvation, and humble upon a colt. John cites it to explain the entry, and reading it whole shows the deliberate choice of a mount that declares peace rather than conquest.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 118:25-26 — Save now, and blessed be he that cometh in the name of the LORD
crossRefs.why: The crowd's "Hosanna" and "Blessed is the King of Israel that cometh in the name of the Lord" come straight from this pilgrim psalm's cry for salvation. The source shows they greeted him with words used to welcome those approaching the temple, now applied to a king.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 53:1 — Lord, who hath believed our report?
crossRefs.why: John quotes this opening question of the suffering servant passage to account for the crowd's refusal to believe. Placed against the chapter it ties the rejection of Jesus to the servant whose glory was hidden in suffering, which is exactly the glory Jesus has just described.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 6:9-10 — seeing they see not, and their hearts are hardened
crossRefs.why: This commission to a people who will look and not perceive is the second passage John cites, and Isaiah receives it within the vision of God's glory in the temple. Reading it explains John's striking remark that the prophet spoke these things "when he saw his glory."

crossRefs.label: Numbers 21:8-9 — the serpent lifted up on a pole, that the bitten might live
crossRefs.why: Moses raises a bronze serpent so that everyone who looks upon it lives. It is the image behind Jesus' language of being "lifted up from the earth," showing that the cross is meant to be looked upon, and that looking is the whole of what the dying are asked to do.

interpretationNotes.claim: Jesus' defense of Mary's costly ointment against the objection that it should have been sold for the poor is read in the Catholic tradition as vindicating lavish, seemingly wasteful honor offered directly to Christ, an instinct the tradition carries into beauty and expense in worship, while insisting that this never stands in competition with real care for the poor.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally stress the uniqueness of the moment: Jesus is bodily present on the eve of his burial, and his words "me ye have not always" mark the act as unrepeatable rather than a general warrant for ornate worship. They more often read the passage as an indictment of Judas' false piety and a call to wholehearted love for Christ. Both traditions agree that devotion to Christ and generosity to the poor are not rivals, and that Jesus honors an act of love which the calculating mind could only see as waste.

interpretationNotes.claim: "I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me" is read in the Catholic tradition as declaring the cross both universally sufficient and universally directed, so that Christ died for all without exception and the drawing is a real grace offered to every person, which grounds the Church's missionary hope while leaving room for a genuine human refusal.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings divide here. Many take "all men" to mean people of every kind, including the Greeks who have just asked to see Jesus, rather than every individual without exception; those in the Reformed stream read the drawing as effectual for those the Father gives him, while others read it as a genuinely universal call. Both traditions agree that the cross is the means by which anyone at all is drawn to Christ, and that the reach of that drawing extends beyond Israel to the nations.

verses.text: Now before the feast of the passover, when Jesus knew that his hour was come that he should depart out of this world unto the Father, having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end.
And supper being ended, the devil having now put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him;
Jesus knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he was come from God, and went to God;
He riseth from supper, and laid aside his garments; and took a towel, and girded himself.
After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples’ feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded.
Then cometh he to Simon Peter: and Peter saith unto him, Lord, dost thou wash my feet?
Jesus answered and said unto him, What I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt know hereafter.
Peter saith unto him, Thou shalt never wash my feet. Jesus answered him, If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me.
Simon Peter saith unto him, Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head.
Jesus saith to him, He that is washed needeth not save to wash his feet, but is clean every whit: and ye are clean, but not all.
For he knew who should betray him; therefore said he, Ye are not all clean.
So after he had washed their feet, and had taken his garments, and was set down again, he said unto them, Know ye what I have done to you?
Ye call me Master and Lord: and ye say well; for so I am.
If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another’s feet.
For I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, The servant is not greater than his lord; neither he that is sent greater than he that sent him.
If ye know these things, happy are ye if ye do them.
I speak not of you all: I know whom I have chosen: but that the scripture may be fulfilled, He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me.
Now I tell you before it come, that, when it is come to pass, ye may believe that I am he.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that receiveth whomsoever I send receiveth me; and he that receiveth me receiveth him that sent me.
When Jesus had thus said, he was troubled in spirit, and testified, and said, Verily, verily, I say unto you, that one of you shall betray me.
Then the disciples looked one on another, doubting of whom he spake.
Now there was leaning on Jesus’ bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved.
Simon Peter therefore beckoned to him, that he should ask who it should be of whom he spake.
He then lying on Jesus’ breast saith unto him, Lord, who is it?
Jesus answered, He it is, to whom I shall give a sop, when I have dipped it. And when he had dipped the sop, he gave it to Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon.
And after the sop Satan entered into him. Then said Jesus unto him, That thou doest, do quickly.
Now no man at the table knew for what intent he spake this unto him.
For some of them thought, because Judas had the bag, that Jesus had said unto him, Buy those things that we have need of against the feast; or, that he should give something to the poor.
He then having received the sop went immediately out: and it was night.
Therefore, when he was gone out, Jesus said, Now is the Son of man glorified, and God is glorified in him.
If God be glorified in him, God shall also glorify him in himself, and shall straightway glorify him.
Little children, yet a little while I am with you. Ye shall seek me: and as I said unto the Jews, Whither I go, ye cannot come; so now I say to you.
A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another.
By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
Simon Peter said unto him, Lord, whither goest thou? Jesus answered him, Whither I go, thou canst not follow me now; but thou shalt follow me afterwards.
Peter said unto him, Lord, why cannot I follow thee now? I will lay down my life for thy sake.
Jesus answered him, Wilt thou lay down thy life for my sake? Verily, verily, I say unto thee, The cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice.

chapters.summary: Before the passover, knowing "that his hour was come that he should depart out of this world unto the Father," Jesus "loved them unto the end." Aware that the Father "had given all things into his hands," he rises from supper, lays aside his garments, girds himself with a towel, and begins washing his disciples' feet. Peter recoils — "Lord, dost thou wash my feet?" then "Thou shalt never wash my feet" — until Jesus warns, "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me," whereupon Peter asks for hands and head as well. Reseated, Jesus explains: "I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you," for "The servant is not greater than his lord." He then names a traitor at his own table, citing the scripture, "He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me." Troubled in spirit, he marks Judas with a dipped sop; "after the sop Satan entered into him," and Judas "went immediately out: and it was night." With the betrayer gone Jesus declares, "Now is the Son of man glorified," and gives "A new commandment... That ye love one another; as I have loved you" — the sign by which "all men know that ye are my disciples." Peter vows to lay down his life and hears instead that he will deny his Lord thrice.
takeaways: The foot washing shows divine authority expressed as service: John notes that Jesus acted precisely because he knew "the Father had given all things into his hands."
Being washed by Christ is not optional courtesy but necessity — "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me" — so cleansing received from him grounds any imitation of him.
The betrayal is foreseen rather than accidental; Jesus announces it beforehand "that, when it is come to pass, ye may believe that I am he."
The "new commandment" sets a new measure for charity, love "as I have loved you," and makes that love the visible identifying mark of his disciples.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 41:9 — mine own familiar friend hath lifted up his heel against me
crossRefs.why: The psalm laments a trusted table companion who turns traitor, the very text Jesus quotes over Judas. Reading it alongside shows the betrayal as the deepest form of the psalmist's grief, and Jesus entering that grief knowingly rather than being surprised by it.

crossRefs.label: Luke 22:24-27 — a strife over greatness at the supper table
crossRefs.why: Luke records the disciples arguing about rank at this same meal, with Jesus answering, "I am among you as he that serveth." The parallel supplies the argument John does not narrate and shows the foot washing as an enacted answer to it.

crossRefs.label: Philippians 2:5-8 — he took upon him the form of a servant
crossRefs.why: Paul describes Christ laying aside equality with God to take a servant's form and obey unto death. The pattern of rising, laying aside garments, and serving matches it closely, so the towel anticipates the cross.

crossRefs.label: 1 John 3:14-18 — he laid down his life for us, and love in deed and in truth
crossRefs.why: The letter treats the new commandment as the test of having passed from death to life, and insists love be practical rather than verbal. It shows how the early Church heard "love one another" as a concrete obligation, not a sentiment.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 26:31-35 — Peter's boast and the prediction of his denial
crossRefs.why: Matthew gives the same exchange with Peter protesting he would die rather than fall away. Set beside John, it underlines that the chapter's teaching on love is addressed to men whose loyalty is about to fail and who will still be kept.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the foot washing is read as more than a moral lesson: it interprets the whole supper, and its ritual reenactment on Holy Thursday ties the humility of the towel to the Eucharist and to the service expected of ordained ministry, so that authority in the Church is defined as washing feet.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the scene as an enacted parable of humble service binding all believers equally, and some traditions practice literal foot washing as an ordinance for the whole congregation rather than a clerical rite. They tend to resist reading a specifically priestly meaning into it. Both traditions agree that Jesus commands his followers to imitate his self-lowering and that greatness among them is measured by service.

interpretationNotes.claim: The distinction in "He that is washed needeth not save to wash his feet, but is clean every whit" is read in the Catholic tradition as touching the difference between the once-only bath of baptism and the repeated cleansing needed for sins committed afterward, which the Church supplies through sacramental confession.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the same distinction as the once-for-all cleansing granted in justification, followed by daily repentance and confession made directly to God rather than through a priest. Some take the verse as simply describing ordinary household custom pressed into service as an image. Both traditions agree that the initial cleansing is entirely Christ's gift and that believers still need ongoing forgiveness from him.

verses.text: Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me.
In my Father’s house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you.
And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you unto myself; that where I am, there ye may be also.
And whither I go ye know, and the way ye know.
Thomas saith unto him, Lord, we know not whither thou goest; and how can we know the way?
Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
If ye had known me, ye should have known my Father also: and from henceforth ye know him, and have seen him.
Philip saith unto him, Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us.
Jesus saith unto him, Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Shew us the Father?
Believest thou not that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? the words that I speak unto you I speak not of myself: but the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works.
Believe me that I am in the Father, and the Father in me: or else believe me for the very works’ sake.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me, the works that I do shall he do also; and greater works than these shall he do; because I go unto my Father.
And whatsoever ye shall ask in my name, that will I do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son.
If ye shall ask any thing in my name, I will do it.
If ye love me, keep my commandments.
And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever;
Even the Spirit of truth; whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth him not, neither knoweth him: but ye know him; for he dwelleth with you, and shall be in you.
I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you.
Yet a little while, and the world seeth me no more; but ye see me: because I live, ye shall live also.
At that day ye shall know that I am in my Father, and ye in me, and I in you.
He that hath my commandments, and keepeth them, he it is that loveth me: and he that loveth me shall be loved of my Father, and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him.
Judas saith unto him, not Iscariot, Lord, how is it that thou wilt manifest thyself unto us, and not unto the world?
Jesus answered and said unto him, If a man love me, he will keep my words: and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him.
He that loveth me not keepeth not my sayings: and the word which ye hear is not mine, but the Father’s which sent me.
These things have I spoken unto you, being yet present with you.
But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you.
Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
Ye have heard how I said unto you, I go away, and come again unto you. If ye loved me, ye would rejoice, because I said, I go unto the Father: for my Father is greater than I.
And now I have told you before it come to pass, that, when it is come to pass, ye might believe.
Hereafter I will not talk much with you: for the prince of this world cometh, and hath nothing in me.
But that the world may know that I love the Father; and as the Father gave me commandment, even so I do. Arise, let us go hence.

chapters.summary: "Let not your heart be troubled," Jesus begins, redirecting the disciples' fear into faith: "ye believe in God, believe also in me." In "my Father’s house are many mansions," and he departs "to prepare a place for you" so that "where I am, there ye may be also." Thomas protests that they know neither the destination nor the road, and receives the chapter's center: "I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me." Philip asks to be shown the Father and is told, "he that hath seen me hath seen the Father," for "I am in the Father, and the Father in me," and "the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works." Believers will do those works and greater, and "whatsoever ye shall ask in my name, that will I do." Love is then defined by obedience — "If ye love me, keep my commandments" — and joined to a promise: the Father will give "another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever; Even the Spirit of truth," who will "teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance." To whoever loves and keeps his word, Father and Son "will come unto him, and make our abode with him." He leaves a parting gift unlike the world's — "my peace I give unto you" — and rises: "Arise, let us go hence."
takeaways: Christ does not merely teach a way to God; he is the way, so access to the Father is personal and passes through him rather than around him.
The chapter grounds the Church's confession of the Son's unity with the Father: "he that hath seen me hath seen the Father," yet the Son is sent, prays to, and returns to the Father.
The promised Comforter is not a substitute for an absent Christ but the mode of his continuing presence: "I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you."
Love for Christ is measured by keeping his word, and it opens into indwelling rather than mere approval: "we will come unto him, and make our abode with him."

crossRefs.label: Exodus 33:18-23 — Moses asks to see God's glory and is told no man can see his face
crossRefs.why: Moses makes the request Philip makes, and is refused the direct sight of God's face. Read alongside, Jesus' answer to Philip is startling: what Moses could not be given is now standing in front of them.

crossRefs.label: Colossians 1:15-19 — the image of the invisible God, in whom all fulness dwells
crossRefs.why: Paul states as doctrine what Jesus states to Philip, that the invisible God is made visible in the Son and dwells in him fully. The pairing shows how quickly the apostolic Church drew the conclusion John records.

crossRefs.label: Acts 2:1-4 — the Spirit given at Pentecost
crossRefs.why: Luke narrates the fulfillment of the promise of "another Comforter" sent in Jesus' name. Reading it alongside turns the promise of this chapter from consolation into recorded event, and explains the disciples' later boldness.

crossRefs.label: Hebrews 9:24 — Christ entered into heaven itself, to appear in the presence of God for us
crossRefs.why: Hebrews describes Christ passing into the heavenly sanctuary on our behalf, which fills out what it means that he goes "to prepare a place for you." The going away is presented as work done for the disciples, not withdrawal from them.

crossRefs.label: Romans 8:9-11 — the Spirit of God dwelling in you
crossRefs.why: Paul speaks of the Spirit dwelling in believers as the pledge of resurrection life, matching the promise that the Spirit "dwelleth with you, and shall be in you" and that "because I live, ye shall live also." It links the indwelling promised here to the hope of bodily life.

interpretationNotes.claim: The Catholic tradition reads "no man cometh unto the Father, but by me" as asserting the unique and universal mediation of Christ, and understands the Church, her sacraments, and the intercession of the saints not as rivals to that mediation but as participations in it, effective only because they are his.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally press the exclusivity of the verse harder, reading it as ruling out any mediating structure between the believer and God and as establishing direct access by faith alone. On this reading, adding intermediaries risks obscuring the sufficiency the verse claims for Christ. Both traditions agree without qualification that there is no other savior and no approach to the Father apart from him.

interpretationNotes.claim: The promise that the Comforter "shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance" is read in the Catholic tradition as a guarantee that the Spirit keeps the apostolic teaching alive and intact in the Church across time, so that the handing on of the faith is itself Spirit-guided and not merely human recollection.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally take the promise as addressed first to the apostles present in the room and fulfilled in the writings they left, so that the Spirit's teaching is now encountered and tested in Scripture. They therefore treat later church teaching as subject to that written witness. Both traditions agree that the Spirit teaches nothing new beyond what Christ himself gave and that his role is to recall the disciples to Jesus' own words.
