verses.text: I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.
Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit.
Now ye are clean through the word which I have spoken unto you.
Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me.
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered; and men gather them, and cast them into the fire, and they are burned.
If ye abide in me, and my words abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you.
Herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit; so shall ye be my disciples.
As the Father hath loved me, so have I loved you: continue ye in my love.
If ye keep my commandments, ye shall abide in my love; even as I have kept my Father’s commandments, and abide in his love.
These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full.
This is my commandment, That ye love one another, as I have loved you.
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
Ye are my friends, if ye do whatsoever I command you.
Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you.

Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit, and that your fruit should remain: that whatsoever ye shall ask of the Father in my name, he may give it you.
These things I command you, that ye love one another.
If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you.
If ye were of the world, the world would love his own: but because ye are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hateth you.
Remember the word that I said unto you, The servant is not greater than his lord. If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they have kept my saying, they will keep yours also.
But all these things will they do unto you for my name’s sake, because they know not him that sent me.
If I had not come and spoken unto them, they had not had sin: but now they have no cloke for their sin.
He that hateth me hateth my Father also.
If I had not done among them the works which none other man did, they had not had sin: but now have they both seen and hated both me and my Father.
But this cometh to pass, that the word might be fulfilled that is written in their law, They hated me without a cause.
But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me:
And ye also shall bear witness, because ye have been with me from the beginning.

chapters.summary: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman." Jesus takes up Israel's oldest image of itself and claims it for himself: barren branches are taken away, and fruitful ones are cut back, "he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit." The command that follows is the chapter's heart: "Abide in me, and I in you," since "the branch cannot bear fruit of itself" and "without me ye can do nothing," while the branch that will not abide "is withered" and burned. Abiding is given concrete shape: his words remaining in them, prayer granted, the Father glorified in "much fruit," and continuance in his love, all spoken "that your joy might be full." The commandment is love "as I have loved you," measured now by the cross: "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." He renames them: "Henceforth I call you not servants... but I have called you friends," and reminds them, "Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you." The tone then turns to warning. The world will hate and persecute them because it hated him first, and its hatred is without excuse — "now they have no cloke for their sin" — fulfilling the word, "They hated me without a cause." Yet the Comforter, "which proceedeth from the Father," will testify of him, and they too shall bear witness.
takeaways: Fruitfulness is never self-generated; it is the life of the vine flowing into the branch, so union with Christ precedes and produces every good work rather than rewarding it.
Pruning is a mark of the Father's care rather than his rejection: even the branch already bearing fruit is cut back so that it may bear more.
Christ's friendship is a gift of election and disclosure, not a wage for achievement — he chose and ordained them and made the Father's counsel known to them.
The world's hostility is predicted and is aimed finally at Christ and his Father, so sharing his mission necessarily means sharing his rejection.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 5:1-7 — the song of the vineyard that brought forth wild grapes
crossRefs.why: Isaiah sings of a lovingly tended vineyard that yields nothing and is left to ruin, naming Israel as the vineyard. Read alongside, Jesus' claim to be "the true vine" answers that failure by locating fruitfulness in himself rather than in the nation.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 80:8-16 — thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt
crossRefs.why: The psalm pictures Israel as a transplanted vine now broken down, and prays that God would visit it again. It supplies the pleading background against which Jesus presents himself as the vine that will not fail.

crossRefs.label: Jeremiah 2:21 — I had planted thee a noble vine, wholly a right seed
crossRefs.why: Jeremiah's single verse condenses the whole complaint: a noble vine has degenerated. Set beside this chapter it sharpens why Jesus adds "true" to "vine" and why abiding, not ancestry, is what bears fruit.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 5:22-23 — the fruit of the Spirit
crossRefs.why: Paul names the fruit that grows where the Spirit is at work, beginning with love. It gives content to the "much fruit" Jesus speaks of and keeps it from being read merely as successful activity.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 69:4 — they that hate me without a cause
crossRefs.why: The psalm of the suffering righteous supplies the phrase Jesus applies to himself, describing groundless hatred from the mighty. The citation places the coming persecution of the disciples inside a long pattern of unjust hostility to God's servants.

interpretationNotes.claim: The Catholic tradition reads the abiding language as describing a real incorporation into Christ that must be maintained and can be lost: the branch is said to be "in me" and yet taken away if it bears no fruit, which supports the understanding that grace requires perseverance and can be forfeited by grave sin, with the sacramental life as the ordinary means of remaining in the vine.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters, especially in the Reformed stream, generally read the fruitless branches as those never truly alive in Christ despite outward attachment, or read the cutting as the Father's chastening rather than final loss, holding that God preserves everyone he genuinely saves. Others take the warning as a real one addressed to the visible church without resolving the question of individual security. Both traditions agree that authentic union with Christ shows itself in fruit and that no one bears any fruit apart from him.

interpretationNotes.claim: That the Spirit is "the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father" while also the one "whom I will send unto you from the Father" is read in the Catholic tradition as pointing to the Spirit's eternal origin from the Father and the Son together, the Son's sending reflecting an inner-divine relation and not merely a task assigned in history.

counterpoint.summary: Western Protestant churches largely retain the same creedal formula, so this is not usually a point of division between them and Catholics. Some Protestant interpreters, however, restrict the verse strictly to the Spirit's mission in time and decline to build a claim about eternal origin on it, treating the question as beyond what the text settles. Both traditions agree that the Spirit comes from the Father and is sent by the risen Son to testify of Christ.

verses.text: These things have I spoken unto you, that ye should not be offended.
They shall put you out of the synagogues: yea, the time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service.
And these things will they do unto you, because they have not known the Father, nor me.
But these things have I told you, that when the time shall come, ye may remember that I told you of them. And these things I said not unto you at the beginning, because I was with you.
But now I go my way to him that sent me; and none of you asketh me, Whither goest thou?
But because I have said these things unto you, sorrow hath filled your heart.
Nevertheless I tell you the truth; It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you.
And when he is come, he will reprove the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment:
Of sin, because they believe not on me;
Of righteousness, because I go to my Father, and ye see me no more;
Of judgment, because the prince of this world is judged.
I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now.

Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak: and he will shew you things to come.
He shall glorify me: for he shall receive of mine, and shall shew it unto you.
All things that the Father hath are mine: therefore said I, that he shall take of mine, and shall shew it unto you.
A little while, and ye shall not see me: and again, a little while, and ye shall see me, because I go to the Father.

Then said some of his disciples among themselves, What is this that he saith unto us, A little while, and ye shall not see me: and again, a little while, and ye shall see me: and, Because I go to the Father?
They said therefore, What is this that he saith, A little while? we cannot tell what he saith.

Now Jesus knew that they were desirous to ask him, and said unto them, Do ye enquire among yourselves of that I said, A little while, and ye shall not see me: and again, a little while, and ye shall see me?
Verily, verily, I say unto you, That ye shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice: and ye shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy.
A woman when she is in travail hath sorrow, because her hour is come: but as soon as she is delivered of the child, she remembereth no more the anguish, for joy that a man is born into the world.
And ye now therefore have sorrow: but I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man taketh from you.
And in that day ye shall ask me nothing. Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, he will give it you.
Hitherto have ye asked nothing in my name: ask, and ye shall receive, that your joy may be full.
These things have I spoken unto you in proverbs: but the time cometh, when I shall no more speak unto you in proverbs, but I shall shew you plainly of the Father.
At that day ye shall ask in my name: and I say not unto you, that I will pray the Father for you:
For the Father himself loveth you, because ye have loved me, and have believed that I came out from God.
I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world: again, I leave the world, and go to the Father.
His disciples said unto him, Lo, now speakest thou plainly, and speakest no proverb.
Now are we sure that thou knowest all things, and needest not that any man should ask thee: by this we believe that thou camest forth from God.
Jesus answered them, Do ye now believe?
Behold, the hour cometh, yea, is now come, that ye shall be scattered, every man to his own, and shall leave me alone: and yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me.
These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.

chapters.summary: Jesus tells them what is coming so that they "should not be offended": expulsion from the synagogues, and death at the hands of men who "will think that he doeth God service," all because "they have not known the Father, nor me." Sorrow has filled their hearts, yet he insists the leaving is gain — "It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you." The Spirit's work is described outward and inward: toward the world he will "reprove the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment"; toward them he will "guide you into all truth," speaking not of himself but taking "of mine" to show them, since "All things that the Father hath are mine." The riddle of "A little while, and ye shall not see me: and again, a little while, and ye shall see me" baffles them, and Jesus answers with a woman in travail whose anguish is forgotten "for joy that a man is born into the world": "your sorrow shall be turned into joy," a joy "no man taketh from you." Prayer changes with it — "ask, and ye shall receive, that your joy may be full" — and speech in "proverbs" will give way to plain words about the Father, who "himself loveth you." They profess faith; he foretells their scattering, then closes: "In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world."
takeaways: Christ presents his own departure as gain rather than loss, since the Spirit's coming depends on his going; the Church is not left poorer by the Ascension but differently endowed.
The Spirit convicts the world and leads the disciples further into truth already given in Christ — "he shall receive of mine" — so no rival or later gospel is to be expected.
Christian sorrow is birth pang rather than defeat: the same hour that scatters and wounds them is the hour that delivers a joy no one can take away.
Forewarning is itself a mercy; Jesus predicts persecution plainly "that when the time shall come, ye may remember that I told you of them."

crossRefs.label: Matthew 10:16-25 — sheep among wolves, scourged in their synagogues
crossRefs.why: Matthew records an earlier and fuller warning of councils, synagogue floggings, and hatred for Jesus' name, with the same principle that the disciple fares as his master did. Read alongside, it shows the persecution of this chapter as a settled expectation of Jesus' teaching rather than a last-minute alarm.

crossRefs.label: Romans 8:18-25 — the whole creation groaneth and travaileth together
crossRefs.why: Paul takes up the same childbirth image for the sufferings of the present age set against the glory to come. It extends Jesus' picture of travail from the disciples' single night of grief to the labor of all creation awaiting deliverance.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 26:17-19 — like a woman in pangs, and thy dead men shall live
crossRefs.why: Isaiah joins the anguish of childbirth to the promise that the dead will rise and sing. The pairing suggests why Jesus reaches for the travail image precisely as he speaks of being unseen and then seen again.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 2:9-13 — the Spirit searcheth the deep things of God
crossRefs.why: Paul describes the Spirit revealing what no human insight could reach and teaching the words in which it is spoken. It illustrates what it means that the Spirit will "guide you into all truth" and speak only what he receives.

crossRefs.label: 1 John 5:4-5 — this is the victory that overcometh the world
crossRefs.why: The letter turns Jesus' closing claim into the believer's share in it, naming faith as the victory over the world. Read together, "I have overcome the world" becomes the ground rather than the mere example of Christian confidence under pressure.

interpretationNotes.claim: The Catholic tradition reads "he will guide you into all truth" as a promise made to the apostolic body and continuing in the Church, so that the Spirit protects the handing on of revelation and permits its genuine unfolding over time without addition to what Christ gave.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally take the promise as addressed to the apostles themselves and fulfilled in the inspired writings that came from them, so that the Spirit's guidance is now recognized and measured by Scripture rather than by a continuing teaching office. Later doctrinal formulations are welcomed on this view only as faithful summaries of that written word. Both traditions agree that the Spirit adds nothing of his own, since he speaks only what is Christ's.

interpretationNotes.claim: "It is expedient for you that I go away" is read in the Catholic tradition as opening the era in which Christ, bodily withdrawn, is nonetheless truly present to his Church through the Spirit in word and sacrament, most fully in the Eucharist, so that his absence is a change of mode rather than a departure.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally understand the promised presence as spiritual presence through the preached word and the indwelling Spirit, with the traditions differing among themselves over how Christ is present in the Supper — some affirming a real but non-localized presence, others a memorial reception by faith. They tend to stress that the Spirit's coming, not a sacramental mode of Christ's body, is what the chapter actually promises. Both traditions agree that Christ's bodily departure does not leave his people alone or unaided.

verses.text: These words spake Jesus, and lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee:
As thou hast given him power over all flesh, that he should give eternal life to as many as thou hast given him.
And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.
I have glorified thee on the earth: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do.
And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was.
I have manifested thy name unto the men which thou gavest me out of the world: thine they were, and thou gavest them me; and they have kept thy word.
Now they have known that all things whatsoever thou hast given me are of thee.
For I have given unto them the words which thou gavest me; and they have received them, and have known surely that I came out from thee, and they have believed that thou didst send me.
I pray for them: I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine.
And all mine are thine, and thine are mine; and I am glorified in them.
And now I am no more in the world, but these are in the world, and I come to thee. Holy Father, keep through thine own name those whom thou hast given me, that they may be one, as we are.
While I was with them in the world, I kept them in thy name: those that thou gavest me I have kept, and none of them is lost, but the son of perdition; that the scripture might be fulfilled.
And now come I to thee; and these things I speak in the world, that they might have my joy fulfilled in themselves.
I have given them thy word; and the world hath hated them, because they are not of the world, even as I am not of the world.
I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil.
They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world.
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
As thou hast sent me into the world, even so have I also sent them into the world.
And for their sakes I sanctify myself, that they also might be sanctified through the truth.
Neither pray I for these alone, but for them also which shall believe on me through their word;
That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me.
And the glory which thou gavest me I have given them; that they may be one, even as we are one:
I in them, and thou in me, that they may be made perfect in one; and that the world may know that thou hast sent me, and hast loved them, as thou hast loved me.
Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am; that they may behold my glory, which thou hast given me: for thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world.
O righteous Father, the world hath not known thee: but I have known thee, and these have known that thou hast sent me.
And I have declared unto them thy name, and will declare it: that the love wherewith thou hast loved me may be in them, and I in them.

chapters.summary: Lifting up his eyes to heaven, Jesus prays: "Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee." He names the gift and its content — "this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent" — reports his work complete, "I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do," and asks to be glorified "with the glory which I had with thee before the world was." He turns to the men given him "out of the world": he has manifested the Father's name, given them his words, and kept them, so that "none of them is lost, but the son of perdition." Departing, he asks the "Holy Father" to "keep through thine own name those whom thou hast given me, that they may be one, as we are," not removing them from the world but keeping "them from the evil," and to "Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth" — for he sends them as he himself was sent, and "for their sakes I sanctify myself." The prayer then widens past the eleven to "them also which shall believe on me through their word," asking "That they all may be one... that the world may believe that thou hast sent me." It ends in desire and love: that they be with him where he is to "behold my glory," and that the Father's love for the Son "may be in them, and I in them."
takeaways: Eternal life is defined here as knowing the Father and the Son he sent, making it a personal communion rather than merely unending existence.

Christ prays as priest for those given him, and the prayer deliberately reaches past the first disciples to all who believe "through their word," so the apostolic witness is the appointed channel of later faith.
The unity asked for is patterned on the oneness of Father and Son and given a missionary purpose — "that the world may believe" — so division is not a private failing but a damaged witness.
Holiness is God's own work through his word, "Sanctify them through thy truth," and it is for sending rather than for withdrawal: they are kept in the world, not taken out of it.

crossRefs.label: Leviticus 16:15-17 — the high priest alone within the veil making atonement for the people
crossRefs.why: The Day of Atonement has the high priest enter the holy place alone, bearing blood and making atonement for himself and for all Israel. Read alongside this prayer, Jesus appears as priest addressing the Father on behalf of those given him, on the eve of offering the sacrifice himself.

crossRefs.label: Hebrews 7:24-25 — he ever liveth to make intercession for them
crossRefs.why: Hebrews describes a priesthood that does not end and an intercession that continues without interruption. It suggests that the prayer of this chapter is not a single night's petition but a window onto what Christ perpetually does.

crossRefs.label: John 1:1-14 — the Word with God in the beginning, and his glory beheld
crossRefs.why: John's prologue asserts the Son's existence with God before creation and the glory seen in his flesh, which is exactly what Jesus asks to have restored, "the glory which I had with thee before the world was." The pairing shows the Gospel closing its frame where it opened it.

crossRefs.label: Ephesians 4:1-6 — one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism
crossRefs.why: Paul turns the oneness Christ prays for into an obligation to be kept and lists what that unity consists of. It gives the petition "that they all may be one" concrete shape in confession, sacrament, and shared life.

crossRefs.label: 1 John 1:1-3 — that ye also may have fellowship with us, and with the Father and the Son
crossRefs.why: The letter's opening describes eyewitnesses declaring what they saw precisely so that later hearers may share their communion. It is the working out of the prayer for "them also which shall believe on me through their word."

interpretationNotes.claim: The Catholic tradition receives this chapter as Christ's priestly prayer, interpreting the cross as an offering rather than merely an execution, and reads "that they all may be one" as asking for a unity that is visible and structured — communion in one faith, one sacramental life, and one order of pastoral care — which is why the healing of Christian division is treated as a duty rather than an optional aspiration.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the requested oneness as the spiritual unity of all who truly belong to Christ, real and already existing across denominational lines rather than identical with any single institutional structure. On this view visible cooperation matters greatly, but organizational union is not what the prayer asks for. Both traditions agree that the unity Christ asks for is not optional and that visible division obscures the very witness the prayer says it should support.

interpretationNotes.claim: "And for their sakes I sanctify myself, that they also might be sanctified through the truth" is read in the Catholic tradition as Christ consecrating himself as both priest and victim, an offering the Church does not repeat but is drawn into, above all in the Eucharist, and from which the consecration of those sent in his name derives.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read "sanctify myself" as Christ setting himself apart for the once-for-all sacrifice of the cross, finished and unrepeatable, with the believer's sanctification following from it through faith and the word of truth. They tend to be wary of any language that could suggest the offering is extended or re-presented. Both traditions agree that the disciples' holiness flows from Christ's self-offering and not from their own effort, and that his work on their behalf is fully sufficient.

verses.text: When Jesus had spoken these words, he went forth with his disciples over the brook Cedron, where was a garden, into the which he entered, and his disciples.
And Judas also, which betrayed him, knew the place: for Jesus ofttimes resorted thither with his disciples.
Judas then, having received a band of men and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, cometh thither with lanterns and torches and weapons.
Jesus therefore, knowing all things that should come upon him, went forth, and said unto them, Whom seek ye?
They answered him, Jesus of Nazareth. Jesus saith unto them, I am he. And Judas also, which betrayed him, stood with them.
As soon then as he had said unto them, I am he, they went backward, and fell to the ground.
Then asked he them again, Whom seek ye? And they said, Jesus of Nazareth.
Jesus answered, I have told you that I am he: if therefore ye seek me, let these go their way:
That the saying might be fulfilled, which he spake, Of them which thou gavest me have I lost none.
Then Simon Peter having a sword drew it, and smote the high priest’s servant, and cut off his right ear. The servant’s name was Malchus.
Then said Jesus unto Peter, Put up thy sword into the sheath: the cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?
Then the band and the captain and officers of the Jews took Jesus, and bound him,
And led him away to Annas first; for he was father in law to Caiaphas, which was the high priest that same year.
Now Caiaphas was he, which gave counsel to the Jews, that it was expedient that one man should die for the people.
And Simon Peter followed Jesus, and so did another disciple: that disciple was known unto the high priest, and went in with Jesus into the palace of the high priest.
But Peter stood at the door without. Then went out that other disciple, which was known unto the high priest, and spake unto her that kept the door, and brought in Peter.
Then saith the damsel that kept the door unto Peter, Art not thou also one of this man’s disciples? He saith, I am not.
And the servants and officers stood there, who had made a fire of coals; for it was cold: and they warmed themselves: and Peter stood with them, and warmed himself.
The high priest then asked Jesus of his disciples, and of his doctrine.
Jesus answered him, I spake openly to the world; I ever taught in the synagogue, and in the temple, whither the Jews always resort; and in secret have I said nothing.
Why askest thou me? ask them which heard me, what I have said unto them: behold, they know what I said.
And when he had thus spoken, one of the officers which stood by struck Jesus with the palm of his hand, saying, Answerest thou the high priest so?
Jesus answered him, If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil: but if well, why smitest thou me?
Now Annas had sent him bound unto Caiaphas the high priest.
And Simon Peter stood and warmed himself. They said therefore unto him, Art not thou also one of his disciples? He denied it, and said, I am not.
One of the servants of the high priest, being his kinsman whose ear Peter cut off, saith, Did not I see thee in the garden with him?
Peter then denied again: and immediately the cock crew.
Then led they Jesus from Caiaphas unto the hall of judgment: and it was early; and they themselves went not into the judgment hall, lest they should be defiled; but that they might eat the passover.
Pilate then went out unto them, and said, What accusation bring ye against this man?
They answered and said unto him, If he were not a malefactor, we would not have delivered him up unto thee.
Then said Pilate unto them, Take ye him, and judge him according to your law. The Jews therefore said unto him, It is not lawful for us to put any man to death:
That the saying of Jesus might be fulfilled, which he spake, signifying what death he should die.
Then Pilate entered into the judgment hall again, and called Jesus, and said unto him, Art thou the King of the Jews?
Jesus answered him, Sayest thou this thing of thyself, or did others tell it thee of me?
Pilate answered, Am I a Jew? Thine own nation and the chief priests have delivered thee unto me: what hast thou done?
Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence.

Pilate therefore said unto him, Art thou a king then? Jesus answered, Thou sayest that I am a king. To this end was I born, and for this cause came I into the world, that I should bear witness unto the truth. Every one that is of the truth heareth my voice.
Pilate saith unto him, What is truth? And when he had said this, he went out again unto the Jews, and saith unto them, I find in him no fault at all.
But ye have a custom, that I should release unto you one at the passover: will ye therefore that I release unto you the King of the Jews?
Then cried they all again, saying, Not this man, but Barabbas. Now Barabbas was a robber.

chapters.summary: Jesus crosses "the brook Cedron" into a garden, where Judas arrives "with lanterns and torches and weapons." Knowing "all things that should come upon him," Jesus goes out to meet them and asks, "Whom seek ye?"; at his answer, "I am he," the band "went backward, and fell to the ground." He shields his own, "if therefore ye seek me, let these go their way," and checks Peter's sword: "the cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?" Bound, he is led first to Annas, father in law to Caiaphas, who had counselled "that it was expedient that one man should die for the people." Outside, Peter warms himself at "a fire of coals" and three times denies him, "and immediately the cock crew." Questioned about his doctrine, Jesus replies that he "spake openly to the world" and "in secret have I said nothing," and when struck he asks, "why smitest thou me?" Delivered to Pilate by accusers who will not enter the judgment hall "lest they should be defiled," he is asked, "Art thou the King of the Jews?" and answers, "My kingdom is not of this world," for "To this end was I born, and for this cause came I into the world, that I should bear witness unto the truth." Pilate's "What is truth?" hangs unanswered; he finds "no fault at all," yet the cry comes, "Not this man, but Barabbas."
takeaways: John's passion begins with Jesus in command, not in collapse: he goes out to his captors, names himself, and gives himself, so that the arrest reads as a free self-offering rather than a defeat.
The cup is received from the Father's hand, and the sword is refused; the kingdom Jesus brings is advanced by witness and obedience, not by force, because it "is not of this world."
Peter's confident loyalty collapses at a servant's question, a reminder that discipleship rests on grace rather than on temperament or nerve.
Truth here is not a theory but a person standing bound before a judge; Pilate's question shows how easily power can hear the truth and still hand it over.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 3:13-14 — I AM THAT I AM, the name revealed at the bush
crossRefs.why: God gives Moses his name as sheer being, the name Israel would not pronounce lightly. Read alongside, Jesus' twice-repeated "I am he," which knocks armed men to the ground, sounds less like simple identification and more like a disclosure of who is really being arrested.

crossRefs.label: John 11:49-52 — Caiaphas counsels that one man should die for the people
crossRefs.why: Caiaphas argues from political calculation that a single death is expedient, and John comments that he prophesied more than he knew. Chapter 18 recalls that counsel precisely as Jesus is bound, so the reader sees a cynical strategy becoming the shape of redemption.

crossRefs.label: John 13:36-38 — Peter promises to lay down his life, and is told he will deny
crossRefs.why: At the supper Peter vows to follow Jesus to death and hears that he will deny him three times before the cock crows. The denial by the coal fire is the exact fulfillment, and it sets up the threefold questioning by another fire in chapter 21.

crossRefs.label: Daniel 7:13-14 — a kingdom given to one like the Son of man
crossRefs.why: Daniel sees dominion granted from heaven to a human figure, an "everlasting dominion" no empire can revoke. It clarifies Jesus' claim before Pilate that he is a king whose kingdom is "not from hence" without being any less real than Rome's.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 26:47-56 — the arrest, the kiss, and the command to sheathe the sword
crossRefs.why: Matthew narrates the same arrest with the betrayer's kiss and the warning that those who take the sword perish by it. The parallel shows what John chooses to emphasize, omitting the agony and the kiss to foreground Jesus' deliberate, sovereign self-surrender.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition Jesus' words about "the cup which my Father hath given me" are read priestly as well as obediently: the passion is a sacrifice he offers rather than merely a fate he suffers, which is why the liturgy speaks of the same offering being made present at the altar.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the cup as the Father's appointed portion of judgment which the Son drinks in the place of sinners, stressing that this offering is complete and unrepeatable once made at Golgotha. The difference concerns how that one sacrifice is applied afterward, not whether it is Christ's own; both traditions affirm that here Jesus freely accepts the Father's will and is not overpowered by his captors.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes Pilate's "What is truth?" as a genuine turning point rather than a witticism: truth is standing before him as a person, so the scene is read as a warning that conscience can recognize innocence and still surrender it to expediency.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters often hear the line as weary Roman cynicism, evidence of a world that has no category for revealed truth apart from God's own testimony. Either way, both traditions read the exchange as John's indictment of a power that declares Jesus faultless and hands him over anyway.

verses.text: Then Pilate therefore took Jesus, and scourged him.
And the soldiers platted a crown of thorns, and put it on his head, and they put on him a purple robe,
And said, Hail, King of the Jews! and they smote him with their hands.
Pilate therefore went forth again, and saith unto them, Behold, I bring him forth to you, that ye may know that I find no fault in him.
Then came Jesus forth, wearing the crown of thorns, and the purple robe. And Pilate saith unto them, Behold the man!
When the chief priests therefore and officers saw him, they cried out, saying, Crucify him, crucify him. Pilate saith unto them, Take ye him, and crucify him: for I find no fault in him.
The Jews answered him, We have a law, and by our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.
When Pilate therefore heard that saying, he was the more afraid;
And went again into the judgment hall, and saith unto Jesus, Whence art thou? But Jesus gave him no answer.
Then saith Pilate unto him, Speakest thou not unto me? knowest thou not that I have power to crucify thee, and have power to release thee?
Jesus answered, Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above: therefore he that delivered me unto thee hath the greater sin.
And from thenceforth Pilate sought to release him: but the Jews cried out, saying, If thou let this man go, thou art not Cæsar’s friend: whosoever maketh himself a king speaketh against Cæsar.
When Pilate therefore heard that saying, he brought Jesus forth, and sat down in the judgment seat in a place that is called the Pavement, but in the Hebrew, Gabbatha.
And it was the preparation of the passover, and about the sixth hour: and he saith unto the Jews, Behold your King!
But they cried out, Away with him, away with him, crucify him. Pilate saith unto them, Shall I crucify your King? The chief priests answered, We have no king but Cæsar.
Then delivered he him therefore unto them to be crucified. And they took Jesus, and led him away.
And he bearing his cross went forth into a place called the place of a skull, which is called in the Hebrew Golgotha:
Where they crucified him, and two other with him, on either side one, and Jesus in the midst.
And Pilate wrote a title, and put it on the cross. And the writing was, JESUS OF NAZARETH THE KING OF THE JEWS.
This title then read many of the Jews: for the place where Jesus was crucified was nigh to the city: and it was written in Hebrew, and Greek, and Latin.
Then said the chief priests of the Jews to Pilate, Write not, The King of the Jews; but that he said, I am King of the Jews.
Pilate answered, What I have written I have written.
Then the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments, and made four parts, to every soldier a part; and also his coat: now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout.

They said therefore among themselves, Let us not rend it, but cast lots for it, whose it shall be: that the scripture might be fulfilled, which saith, They parted my raiment among them, and for my vesture they did cast lots. These things therefore the soldiers did.
Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene.
When Jesus therefore saw his mother, and the disciple standing by, whom he loved, he saith unto his mother, Woman, behold thy son!
Then saith he to the disciple, Behold thy mother! And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home.
After this, Jesus knowing that all things were now accomplished, that the scripture might be fulfilled, saith, I thirst.
Now there was set a vessel full of vinegar: and they filled a spunge with vinegar, and put it upon hyssop, and put it to his mouth.
When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.

The Jews therefore, because it was the preparation, that the bodies should not remain upon the cross on the sabbath day, ( for that sabbath day was an high day,) besought Pilate that their legs might be broken, and that they might be taken away.
Then came the soldiers, and brake the legs of the first, and of the other which was crucified with him.
But when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was dead already, they brake not his legs:
But one of the soldiers with a spear pierced his side, and forthwith came there out blood and water.
And he that saw it bare record, and his record is true: and he knoweth that he saith true, that ye might believe.
For these things were done, that the scripture should be fulfilled, A bone of him shall not be broken.
And again another scripture saith, They shall look on him whom they pierced.

And after this Joseph of Arimathaea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, besought Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus: and Pilate gave him leave. He came therefore, and took the body of Jesus.
And there came also Nicodemus, which at the first came to Jesus by night, and brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about an hundred pound weight.
Then took they the body of Jesus, and wound it in linen clothes with the spices, as the manner of the Jews is to bury.
Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden; and in the garden a new sepulchre, wherein was never man yet laid.
There laid they Jesus therefore because of the Jews’ preparation day; for the sepulchre was nigh at hand.

chapters.summary: Pilate scourges Jesus; the soldiers plait "a crown of thorns" and a "purple robe" and mock him, "Hail, King of the Jews!" Pilate presents him with "Behold the man!" and repeats, "I find no fault in him," but the charge escalates: "he made himself the Son of God." More afraid, Pilate asks, "Whence art thou?" and receives no answer, then hears that his own authority is only "given thee from above." Cornered by "We have no king but Cæsar," he sits at the Pavement, says "Behold your King!" and delivers him up. Jesus goes "bearing his cross" to Golgotha and is crucified between two others, with Pilate's trilingual title fixed above him and unretracted: "What I have written I have written." The soldiers divide his garments and cast lots for the seamless coat, "that the scripture might be fulfilled." Standing by the cross are his mother and other women; to her he says, "Woman, behold thy son!" and to the beloved disciple, "Behold thy mother!" Knowing "that all things were now accomplished," he says "I thirst," receives vinegar on hyssop, declares "It is finished," and "gave up the ghost." His legs are not broken, but a spear pierces his side and "forthwith came there out blood and water" — scripture fulfilled twice over. Joseph of Arimathaea and Nicodemus bury him with myrrh and aloes in a garden tomb "wherein was never man yet laid."
takeaways: John frames the crucifixion as enthronement: the thorns, the robe, the title in three languages, and the twice-spoken "Behold your King" all say in mockery what the evangelist means in earnest.
"It is finished" is a word of completion rather than exhaustion; the work given him is accomplished, and he then hands over his life rather than having it merely taken.
The unbroken bones and the pierced side are presented as deliberate fulfillments, tying Jesus to the paschal lamb and to the prophetic promise that Israel would look upon the one they pierced.
From the cross Jesus establishes a bond of care between his mother and the disciple, so that even in dying he is forming the household of those who belong to him.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 22:16-18 — they pierced my hands and feet and cast lots for my garments
crossRefs.why: The psalm describes a righteous sufferer surrounded by enemies, his bones exposed and his clothing divided by lot. John quotes it directly at the dividing of the garments, so the whole psalm becomes a script the crucifixion is visibly following.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 53:3-7 — despised and rejected, wounded for our transgressions, and silent before his accusers
crossRefs.why: Isaiah portrays a servant who is disfigured, bears the iniquity of others, and opens not his mouth. It illuminates both Jesus' silence when Pilate demands "Whence art thou?" and John's insistence that this death is substitutionary and willed, not accidental.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 12:43-46 — the passover lamb, of which no bone shall be broken
crossRefs.why: The law of the passover forbids breaking a bone of the lamb whose blood spares Israel. John notes the hour of preparation, the hyssop that once applied the blood, and the unbroken legs, presenting Jesus as the true paschal lamb dying as the passover lambs are being readied.

crossRefs.label: Zechariah 12:10 — they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and mourn
crossRefs.why: Zechariah promises an outpoured spirit of grace and a people who look on the pierced one and grieve. John cites it at the spear thrust, so the wound becomes not merely proof of death but the object of a repentant, believing gaze.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 3:15 — the woman, her seed, and the promise of a crushed serpent
crossRefs.why: The first promise of deliverance is given to "the woman" and her offspring, not to Eve by name. In the Catholic tradition this is read against Jesus addressing his mother as "Woman" at the cross, seeing the promise reaching its completion at the very moment the serpent's work appears to triumph.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the words "Woman, behold thy son" and "Behold thy mother" are read as more than a dying son arranging his mother's care: because Jesus addresses her by title rather than by name and the disciple is left unnamed, Mary is understood to be given as mother to all who are beloved disciples, which is the scriptural root of Catholic devotion to her as mother of the Church.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the exchange at its plainest level, as a genuine act of filial duty in which Jesus entrusts a widowed mother to a trusted disciple who "took her unto his own home," and they are cautious about extending a specific household arrangement into a universal spiritual relationship. Both traditions honor Mary's fidelity in standing at the cross when almost everyone else had fled, and both see Jesus caring for his own to the very end.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading treats the "blood and water" from the pierced side as a sacramental sign as well as a medical detail, seeing in it the Eucharist and baptism flowing from the opened side of Christ, which is why the Church is described as born from the cross.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally take the blood and water first as the eyewitness proof John says it is, "his record is true: and he knoweth that he saith true, that ye might believe," establishing that Jesus was really dead against any suggestion of a swoon. Many also allow a secondary symbolism of cleansing and life, so the traditions differ over emphasis and sacramental weight rather than over the plain claim that a real death has really been witnessed.

verses.text: The first day of the week cometh Mary Magdalene early, when it was yet dark, unto the sepulchre, and seeth the stone taken away from the sepulchre.

Then she runneth, and cometh to Simon Peter, and to the other disciple, whom Jesus loved, and saith unto them, They have taken away the Lord out of the sepulchre, and we know not where they have laid him.
Peter therefore went forth, and that other disciple, and came to the sepulchre.
So they ran both together: and the other disciple did outrun Peter, and came first to the sepulchre.
And he stooping down, and looking in, saw the linen clothes lying; yet went he not in.
Then cometh Simon Peter following him, and went into the sepulchre, and seeth the linen clothes lie,
And the napkin, that was about his head, not lying with the linen clothes, but wrapped together in a place by itself.
Then went in also that other disciple, which came first to the sepulchre, and he saw, and believed.
For as yet they knew not the scripture, that he must rise again from the dead.
Then the disciples went away again unto their own home.
But Mary stood without at the sepulchre weeping: and as she wept, she stooped down, and looked into the sepulchre,
And seeth two angels in white sitting, the one at the head, and the other at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain.
And they say unto her, Woman, why weepest thou? She saith unto them, Because they have taken away my Lord, and I know not where they have laid him.
And when she had thus said, she turned herself back, and saw Jesus standing, and knew not that it was Jesus.

Jesus saith unto her, Woman, why weepest thou? whom seekest thou? She, supposing him to be the gardener, saith unto him, Sir, if thou have borne him hence, tell me where thou hast laid him, and I will take him away.
Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master.
Jesus saith unto her, Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father: but go to my brethren, and say unto them, I ascend unto my Father, and your Father; and to my God, and your God.
Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had spoken these things unto her.

Then the same day at evening, being the first day of the week, when the doors were shut where the disciples were assembled for fear of the Jews, came Jesus and stood in the midst, and saith unto them, Peace be unto you.
And when he had so said, he shewed unto them his hands and his side. Then were the disciples glad, when they saw the Lord.
Then said Jesus to them again, Peace be unto you: as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you.
And when he had said this, he breathed on them, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost:
Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained.
But Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came.

The other disciples therefore said unto him, We have seen the Lord. But he said unto them, Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe.
And after eight days again his disciples were within, and Thomas with them: then came Jesus, the doors being shut, and stood in the midst, and said, Peace be unto you.
Then saith he to Thomas, Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.
And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.
Jesus saith unto him, Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.
And many other signs truly did Jesus in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book:
But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name.

chapters.summary: On "the first day of the week," while it is "yet dark," Mary Magdalene finds the stone taken away and runs to Peter and the beloved disciple: "They have taken away the Lord out of the sepulchre." The two race there; the other disciple arrives first but waits, Peter enters and sees "the linen clothes" with the napkin "wrapped together in a place by itself," and then the first disciple "saw, and believed," though "as yet they knew not the scripture." Mary remains weeping, sees two angels who ask, "Woman, why weepest thou?" and mistakes Jesus for "the gardener" until he speaks one word, "Mary," and she answers, "Rabboni." He sends her to "my brethren" with the message, "I ascend unto my Father, and your Father; and to my God, and your God." That evening, behind shut doors, Jesus stands among them: "Peace be unto you," shows "his hands and his side," commissions them, "as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you," then "he breathed on them" saying, "Receive ye the Holy Ghost: Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted." Thomas, absent, demands to touch the wounds; eight days later Jesus returns and invites him, "be not faithless, but believing," drawing the confession, "My Lord and my God," and the blessing on "they that have not seen, and yet have believed." John closes by naming his purpose: these signs are written "that ye might believe."
takeaways: Faith here begins from evidence but is not reducible to it: the folded burial cloths, the wounds, and the spoken name each invite belief, yet the blessing falls on those who believe without seeing.
Thomas' "My Lord and my God" is the plainest confession of Jesus' divinity in the Gospel, and it is spoken to the risen body that still bears its wounds.
The risen Christ hands on his own mission, "even so send I you," so the Church's authority is derived rather than self-generated, breathed into it by the Spirit.
The commission includes the forgiveness of sins, joining the gift of peace to the concrete task of releasing people from what binds them.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 2:7 — the LORD breathes into man and he becomes a living soul
crossRefs.why: At creation God forms man from dust and breathes life into him. When Jesus "breathed on them" and gives the Holy Ghost, the deliberate echo presents Easter evening as a new creation, the risen Lord animating a renewed humanity.

crossRefs.label: Luke 24:36-43 — Jesus stands among them, greets them with peace, and shows his hands and feet
crossRefs.why: Luke narrates the same evening appearance with the greeting of peace, the display of wounds, and the eating of food to prove he is no spirit. The independent parallel strengthens the claim that the resurrection is bodily and physically verifiable.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 18:15-18 — whatsoever ye shall bind on earth shall be bound in heaven
crossRefs.why: Matthew places binding and loosing in the setting of reconciling a sinning brother within the community. Read with John's "Whose soever sins ye remit," it shows the same authority described in two registers, disciplinary and forgiving, and given to those Jesus sends.

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 5:18-20 — the ministry and word of reconciliation committed to us
crossRefs.why: Paul describes God committing to his messengers a ministry of reconciliation, so that they plead in Christ's stead for people to be reconciled. Protestant interpreters often read John's commission through this lens, as the entrusting of the announcement of forgiveness rather than a private judicial power.

crossRefs.label: 1 John 1:1-3 — that which we have heard, seen, and our hands have handled
crossRefs.why: The letter grounds its testimony in what was physically seen and touched of "the Word of life." It reads as the settled reflection of the same witness who recorded Thomas being invited to reach out his hand, insisting that Christian claims rest on tangible encounter.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the breathing of the Spirit with the words "Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained" is read as Christ instituting a real power of absolution entrusted to the apostles and their successors, which is why the Church practices sacramental confession with an ordained minister pronouncing forgiveness.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the words as authorizing the Church to declare God's forgiveness through the faithful preaching of the gospel, binding where the message is refused and loosing where it is believed, and they hold that God alone forgives sin without a human intermediary being required. Both traditions affirm that the risen Christ genuinely gives his Church a Spirit-empowered authority to announce forgiveness in his name, and that no one forgives apart from him.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading gives weight to Jesus' blessing on "they that have not seen, and yet have believed" as the charter for faith transmitted through witnesses rather than direct sight, which supports the Catholic understanding that Scripture and the living tradition of the apostolic community together hand on what Thomas saw.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally connect the same blessing to John's stated purpose in the closing verses, that the written signs are recorded "that ye might believe," and so locate the sufficient witness in Scripture itself. Both traditions agree that later believers depend entirely on apostolic testimony rather than private appearances, and that such faith is not second-class but blessed.

verses.text: After these things Jesus shewed himself again to the disciples at the sea of Tiberias; and on this wise shewed he himself.
There were together Simon Peter, and Thomas called Didymus, and Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two other of his disciples.
Simon Peter saith unto them, I go a fishing. They say unto him, We also go with thee. They went forth, and entered into a ship immediately; and that night they caught nothing.
But when the morning was now come, Jesus stood on the shore: but the disciples knew not that it was Jesus.
Then Jesus saith unto them, Children, have ye any meat? They answered him, No.
And he said unto them, Cast the net on the right side of the ship, and ye shall find. They cast therefore, and now they were not able to draw it for the multitude of fishes.

Therefore that disciple whom Jesus loved saith unto Peter, It is the Lord. Now when Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he girt his fisher’s coat unto him, ( for he was naked,) and did cast himself into the sea.
And the other disciples came in a little ship; ( for they were not far from land, but as it were two hundred cubits,) dragging the net with fishes.
As soon then as they were come to land, they saw a fire of coals there, and fish laid thereon, and bread.
Jesus saith unto them, Bring of the fish which ye have now caught.
Simon Peter went up, and drew the net to land full of great fishes, an hundred and fifty and three: and for all there were so many, yet was not the net broken.
Jesus saith unto them, Come and dine. And none of the disciples durst ask him, Who art thou? knowing that it was the Lord.
Jesus then cometh, and taketh bread, and giveth them, and fish likewise.
This is now the third time that Jesus shewed himself to his disciples, after that he was risen from the dead.
So when they had dined, Jesus saith to Simon Peter, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these? He saith unto him, Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my lambs.
He saith to him again the second time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? He saith unto him, Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my sheep.

He saith unto him the third time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? Peter was grieved because he said unto him the third time, Lovest thou me? And he said unto him, Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee. Jesus saith unto him, Feed my sheep.

Verily, verily, I say unto thee, When thou wast young, thou girdedst thyself, and walkedst whither thou wouldest: but when thou shalt be old, thou shalt stretch forth thy hands, and another shall gird thee, and carry thee whither thou wouldest not.
This spake he, signifying by what death he should glorify God. And when he had spoken this, he saith unto him, Follow me.
Then Peter, turning about, seeth the disciple whom Jesus loved following; which also leaned on his breast at supper, and said, Lord, which is he that betrayeth thee?
Peter seeing him saith to Jesus, Lord, and what shall this man do?
Jesus saith unto him, If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me.
Then went this saying abroad among the brethren, that that disciple should not die: yet Jesus said not unto him, He shall not die; but, If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee?
This is the disciple which testifieth of these things, and wrote these things: and we know that his testimony is true.
And there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written. Amen.

chapters.summary: At the sea of Tiberias seven disciples are together when Peter says, "I go a fishing," and "that night they caught nothing." At dawn an unrecognized figure on the shore asks, "Children, have ye any meat?" and tells them, "Cast the net on the right side of the ship, and ye shall find"; the haul is so great they cannot draw it. The beloved disciple says, "It is the Lord," and Peter throws himself into the sea. On land they find "a fire of coals" with "fish laid thereon, and bread," and Peter drags in the net holding "an hundred and fifty and three" great fishes, "yet was not the net broken." Jesus says, "Come and dine," and none dare ask who he is. After the meal he questions Peter three times, "Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?"; Peter, grieved by the third asking, answers, "Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee," and each time receives a charge: "Feed my lambs," "Feed my sheep," "Feed my sheep." Jesus then foretells that when Peter is old "another shall gird thee, and carry thee whither thou wouldest not," signifying "by what death he should glorify God," and says simply, "Follow me." When Peter asks about the beloved disciple, Jesus answers, "what is that to thee? follow thou me," correcting a rumor. The Gospel ends attesting that disciple's testimony and confessing that the world could not contain all Jesus did.
takeaways: Restoration is personal and unhurried: the threefold questioning by a charcoal fire answers the threefold denial by another charcoal fire, healing the failure at the place where it happened.
Peter is not merely forgiven but commissioned; love for Christ is immediately translated into responsibility for Christ's flock, which remains his and not the shepherd's.
Following Jesus includes the cost he foretells, so that Peter's future death is described not as tragedy but as a way to "glorify God."
Curiosity about another disciple's path is gently refused, "follow thou me," a reminder that vocation is given individually and not measured against someone else's.

crossRefs.label: Luke 5:1-11 — the great catch at Jesus' word and the call to catch men
crossRefs.why: Luke records a night of empty nets, a command to let down the net, an overwhelming haul, and Peter's collapse before Jesus, followed by his call. The resurrection scene deliberately repeats that pattern, so Peter's commissioning by the sea comes full circle after his denial.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 16:17-19 — Simon Barjona, the rock, and the keys of the kingdom
crossRefs.why: Jesus there addresses Peter by his father's name, renames him, and entrusts him with keys and with binding and loosing. In the Catholic tradition John 21 is read as the fulfillment of that promise, Jesus again using "Simon, son of Jonas" as he places the flock in his care.

crossRefs.label: John 10:11-16 — the good shepherd who lays down his life, one fold and one shepherd
crossRefs.why: Jesus identifies himself as the shepherd who owns the sheep and dies for them, unlike the hireling who flees. Reading it beside "Feed my sheep" shows Peter being made an under-shepherd of a flock that always belongs to Christ, and being told his own death will follow the shepherd's pattern.

crossRefs.label: Ezekiel 34:11-16 — I will seek my sheep and feed them, says the LORD
crossRefs.why: Ezekiel condemns shepherds who feed themselves and promises that God himself will gather and feed the flock. It sets Jesus' charge to Peter inside a long prophetic argument about who may be trusted with God's people and on what terms.

crossRefs.label: 1 Peter 5:1-4 — feed the flock of God, not for filthy lucre, under the chief Shepherd
crossRefs.why: Peter writes to elders urging them to shepherd God's flock willingly and without lording it over them, awaiting "the chief Shepherd." It reads as Peter passing on the very charge he received on the shore, and it shows how he himself understood it.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition the threefold "Feed my sheep" is read as the risen Christ conferring on Peter a genuine pastoral office over the whole flock, not simply reinstating a forgiven friend, and this passage together with the promise of the keys grounds the Catholic understanding of a Petrine ministry of unity continued in his successors.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the scene primarily as Peter's personal restoration after his three denials, returning him to the apostolic ministry he shares equally with the others, and they note that Peter himself later addresses fellow elders as an elder among them rather than as their ruler. Both traditions affirm that Jesus fully restores Peter, entrusts him with real responsibility for God's people, and remains himself the one Shepherd to whom the flock belongs.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes the unbroken net full of a specific, countable number of great fishes as an image of the Church's catholicity and unity: the mission gathers people of every kind, and the net that Peter draws to land does not tear.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters are generally more restrained about the number itself, treating it as the vivid recollection of an eyewitness and reading the abundance simply as evidence of the risen Lord's power to make the disciples' mission fruitful where their own effort caught nothing. Both traditions read the scene as a promise about mission, that the gathering succeeds at Christ's word and not by the fishermen's skill.
